div.p: TO THE ELECTORS OF THE BOROUGH OF
WARRINGTON.

GENTLEMEN —Having been selected by the General Council of the Liberal Association to succeed your old friend, Mr. McMionlee, whose retirement from Parliamentary life 1,1 ke yourselves, deeply regret. I now offer my;elf for your suffrages. and, if I should succeed by your favour in obtaining the seat which is shout to be vacated. I shall always endeavour faith- fully to represent your Borough in tbe House of Commons. The prompt attention of the New Parliament will necerarrily be given to the improvement of the present mode of transact- irg public business, which has of late been unwarrantly ob- structeri in the Lower House, whilst the persistent opposition to pnpular measures by the 'rouse of Lords, will, if continued. bring about a 'antral change in that branch of the Leelrla- Cure.
In the treatment of Foreign Affsirs, it is my opinion that the Interests of our widespread possessions should be daiefully protected, with a due regard to the just rights of our neigh- bours.

In dealing with the Colonies, where so many of our own flesh ard blood have found new homes. I consider that our policy should be to maintain the unity of the Empire, while preserving these prinsiples of self-goverment which moot of cur dependencies have developed in so marked a manner. The system adopted by the late Adminii•tratAon in the Government of India has been so conspicuously successful In obtaining the goodwill of the subject races, that I hope to see It further devel ped in the direction of allowing duly qualified natives to perform the full share in the duties of the execu- tive, and thus ensure.. that CollfirieflC•3 which is the only permanent bond between us and our greatest Dependency Inasmuch as the new Rouse of Commons will be the first in our tistory elected by th vides sf the entire nation. I lonic forward with hops to the discussion in the corning sessions, • f the numerous problems which concern the physical and moral well-being of our tiwn population in the new light wh th wili be brought to bear upon them by the chosen representatives the new electors. I believe It is the highest function of Per- lisa ant to enact such laws as shall redress the stooges-which still linger among us, and also to extend to those classes who. being hi, herto unrepresented, have net had their full share of consideration, the benefi,s which past legislation has secured for those who have already exercised the frftrichLe. I there- fore consider that a large portion of the time of Perliossent will be well spent in pass ng measures of domestic ut.lity. Among these I would place Licensing Reform, which in my Opinion shosid not stop short ef a taw giving to the rate- payers the power to regulate the issue of public-house licenses This will no doubt form a branch ot the greater question of Local Government, wirch whether it concerns London or vil- lage communities, requ'res early s ,ttlement, and must ems brace the three kingdoms. In Irel.nd, particularly, it is to be expected that the energy which will be called forth by the long delayed enlianehisement, alike of town and country voters, will find a profitable outlet in the perfecting of load institutions; and I am therefore in favour of granting to the Sister Isle the greatest possible measure o. sellgovera- =mt.
t Ilak ent

The representatives of •agricultural constituencies will urge the Immediate alteration of existing laws relating to /and, and the enactment of a measute which, by simplifying the mrde of tranfer, WI I enable g sellers readily to treat with those who w .uld buy if legal obstsves were not imposed. Other ouesVons, such as primogeniture, entail, arts settlemem, must follow and a satisftwtory con- clusion will no doubt be more easily arrived at when the nominal owners find that unfettered land is a marketable com- modity. Any mea,ure calculated to attain this end shall have my hearty support. The Disestablishment of the Scotch and Welsh Churches is a que.li os of the near future, whilst the equalisation of all forms of religion, In the eye of the law, as it already exists in our Colonies, must ere long be acc.mplish d Is. England The quel.t on of Elementary Educat'on is involved in so , much difficulty, each view being supported by equally earnest advocates. th.t I should desire to see It thoroughly oiscussed. steps being taken meanwhile to facilitate the remission of fee's, In all cases where parents are unable to pay them In such x way as shall prevent any tense of humiliation. As regards the maintenance of Voluntary Schools, I am prepared to further an inquiry having for its object the removal of such inequalities as exi-t between them an.. B ard Schools. The tendency to increase expenditure, which is natural to the spending departments ot the public service, most be st-en- uously opposed, but this can only be done by the earnest efforte on the part of inchvldual members with the support of their oonstirueuts„ whose money is too frequently spent on a coal e which is calculated to satisfy the demands of the receiver rather Own the means of the taxpayer. lam aware that there are numerous questions of interest I to many of y.. 0 which I have not touched upon, fearing to ! make this address too long. hut, as I shall have opportunities , of meeling you before the day of the election, I must defer I particular reference to them till then. Other subjects nor, now be! re the country, but which may be brought before Parliament, I shall, if elected, consider in I the broad spirit of that advancing Liheralism which bas done so much for this country Is. the past. Bo far as it is neces- sary to attach m self to any one man, I desire to take my place among those wr.o follow our veteran leader, G ad- stone, as long as he is willing to place himself at the head of the party with whose co-opera, ion he has been enabled to con- ler so many benefits upon the natio,s at large. I remain, gentlemen, Your obedient servant. WILLIAM CROdNIELD. October 22nd, 1885.
- -- TO THE ELECTORS OF -THE NEWTON DIVISION OF LAROABIIIIIE.

GENTLEMEN,— Six mon, hs have now passed since the com- mittees of the Liberal party did me the honour of inviting me to become the candidate, in the Liberal interest, for the New. ton Division of Lancashire, where I have resided the greater pa, t of my life.

should you cold= this expression of c mfidence in me by securing my election fur your Division, under the operation of the New Franchise Act, it will be my endeavour to devote my time, and such experience as I possess, to the furtherance of the best interests of the great Liberal cause.

roc by cimviction I belong to the party that reirgnizes Me. Gladstone as Its leader, and believing that the views which occupy a prominent, position in his "Manifesto," are best cal- culated to nromote toe welfare of the nation at large, and those sections of the community in hose behalf leittsiation seems to me t) be specially needed, I should give my hearty support to the rneasuiee which that Illustrious ststes- man has advocated.

Hain g from my earliest years been a member o' the Church either under the form estahished in lcotlad or mader that of the Church of England, I deprecate any attempt to sever the connection between Church and State, 'which has so leng existed to the benefit of rogation and to the blessing of the people. At the same lime I should be glad to further any salutary reforms whereby the National Church should be the better able to discharge her duties to the people. And, as heretofore during my whole llfe, I am anxious to .ee and to encourage healthy yet chiritabte emulation between the vari- OUS Christian denominations and the Established Church.

I thoroughly approve of the proposal to institute County Boards, as being iii the nature of things best qualified to d's- charge local busin es, wl, h due regard to local in erest, with more promptitude and efficiency than can be expected from the Imperial Parliament. The present system of granting and with-holding L eenSe9 is generally admitted to be unsatisfac- tory ai.dde.ective, and it is believed twit a County Board, with its knowledge of the wants of the neighborhood, would be well qualifl d to grant Licensee in future, as well as to have the power of withholding them. I trust that the present system of education conducted In our denomi-atlonal schools will not be disturbed, but I would like to see some change in the manner of assisting those parents who are unable to pay the fees. _

I believe that all agree in the necessity of altering the laws affecting land. It shOu dbe made as free and t an-ferab le as that of any commodity. it Is anticipatei that the changes will be beneficial alike dirtrtly to the landowner, the tenant, the farm labourer, and I believe, by the increased productive- rums of the roll, Indirectly to the country at large. The time cann t be far distant yob en the reform of the House of Lords must be carefully brought forward so as to prevent the Eleroditary Chamber from thwarting the well-considered decisions of the Representative Chamber, the Commons House of Parliament. I have always been heartily in favour of Free Trade, and would oppose any return to a policy of Protecion. It shall be my ithltiellS desire to watch carefully over the Interest; of Agriculture nod Trade, and , the safety and well• being of our Miners and Bailors, to whose courage and indus- try we are largely indebted for much of the prosperity and wealth of the Empire, as well as toe comfort of the whole community, and their no upations being attended with con- siderable risk, fresh legislation in their 'shalt is demandets I consider the efficiency of the Army and Navy all-important for the protection of cur Country and Corobles, but not fer unnecessary interference with roteign Nations. Deploring as I do the troubles arid sufferings that still pre- vail in Ireland. I am prepared to cordially welcome and sup- port such good measures as may be brought forward in the in'erest of our ini-h fellow-countrymen, who are certainly entitled to All the privileges which rue enju) ed by the rest of the United Kingdom. Antic pating the carrying out of these and other imprvtarit mew urea. I approve of amending the rules of the Hurls, of Commons so as to prevent obstruction and secure the proper discussion and consideration of 11 subjects that may be brought under its notice There are other topics that will require attention, and as I expect shortly to have the pleasure of meeting' you in the various Districts of the Division, we shall have ripportu- :titles of exchanging our views regarding all important measures - - . .

cor chn.lon I will only briefly state that my aim, if I shruld be to fortu: ate as to obtain 3tir suffrages, will be to labour for the best Interests of the United Blngdom of Great Br Lal n and Ire' nd and our Colonies, withcut losing sight of these special claims upan my loyal service which would de- volve up .n me RS your nepresentative. I have the honour to be, Gentlemen, Your faithful &Avant, • GEORGE MCCORQUOD kLE. The Willows, Newton-le-Willows, October 20th, 1883.
TO THE ELECTORS OF EAST SUTTON WARD.

LADIFS AND GENTLEVEN,—A Ye-caney will shortly occur in the repre.entratlou of your Ward, through the retirement of Mr. Councillor Mass-y. 1 have been requested to allow my name to be put in nomination for the vacancy, and have pleasure in acceding t. the reuuest. Should you do me the honour of ele ting me aa yonr Representative, 1 shall always consider that the affairs of the Corporation require the same attention and economy Fut t brae of a private business; yvhile as a Representative of your Ward, it will be my duty to have a special regard to the interests and necessities of k ast Button. I a.n in favour of the Branch Library movement, and or all measures for the pramotion of the social wed-being of the inhabitants of tie district. I have the honour to be. . Ladles and Gentlemen. Your obedient Servant, Bold Wsrlis, Bt. Helens Junction, October 10th, 18S6. R. o. awnA.ans.

The question of free primary educa ion has come rapidly to the front. and It will, I hope, be fettled before tang in accord- ance with the wishes of thoee who support It. It has been tried with satisfactory results in the vast majority of ether civil'sed countries, and I do not see any reason to suppose that its adoption would prejudicially affect denominational schools. The somewhat difficult matter of the application of funds which have been left for various objPcts now no longer exist- ent, owing to the altered eircumstaoces under which we live, sr which, if existent, do not derive the benefit which was in- tended, mukt soon come up for s,ttb.inent. I feel that the short period for which you did me the honour of e acting me to fill the vacancy whim lstely ocaurred in the remresentation Of your Ward, scarce se afforded me much op- portunity of representing your interests; but at the same time 1 trust the attention I gave to the general business of the town met With your approval. The further improvement in the sanitary arrangements of the Borough is being brought before the notice of the Corpora- tion by the Authorit,es in Loudon, and their suggesdons de- mend the closest scrutiny, in order to prevent increased ex- penditure. The completion of the works for the Increased water supply, and many -ther matters of the greatest import- ance to the welfare of our rapidly-increasing town, shall, if you again honour me with your confidence, have my constant and careful attention. I have the honour to be, Ladles and taentlemen. Your obedient Servant. EDWARD JOHNSON.

• SHAFTESBURY. Vita pulcherrimus; Mors gloriosna ;.uus nomen benedicito manes servi Dei. How beautiful hath his probation been, How full oesacred thoughts, and how serene The great transition. Shaftesbury liv'd to show The blessedness of lives which seek to throw , A halo o'er the world. He wearied not In striving to erase each lurid blot That kept, 0 Christ, thy little ones afar From thee their joy, their Hopo and Comfort's star. He for the lowly children of his land, Delighted as a champion true to stand, To utilise his influence and his name For higher ends than glowing statesman's fame. His statesmanship was such as wins a place Amongst the peers of more celestial race. And thus is he translated from earth's sod, To peerage in the Upper House of God. Where coronets last longer and retain, A brightness never dimto'd by grief and pain. He rests—he who succeeded mrhis aim, To save our infant souls from want and shame. His voice is hush'd, yet other voices nigh, , His works of goodness long will magnify. And spirit realms his union now will bless, With those who once enrich'd his happiness. Yes, they were thine, 0 Christ, those little ones, Be sought to succour—daughters fair, and sons Who never heard the music of the spheres; Who never saw the flowery mead which ceers, The soaring bird more oft than human eyes. Deprived of natural bliss and sunny skies; He led them on, took each one by the hand, And led them upward to their Fatherland! So new existence on them davrn'd, and now In sorrow not unmix'd with joy they bow. They weave a chaplet for their earthly lord, And say to day "How great is his reward !" They may not speak their loss, for loss like this, . No stimulus for future toil shall miss, Then muse, 0 cast this tribute in the tomb'. Of him whose death removes from death all gloom. --Cerro.

div.head: SCIENCE, ART, &c.
div.p: SCIENCE, ART, &c.
M. Pasteur is at his 'country retreat in the Jura, per- fecting a methodfor assuring to animals exemption from hydrophobia, which will also be. efficacious ia the case of mare. _ _ .

A tomb has been discovered atfianagra, with its walls covered with encaustic paintings of great tad:a-deal skill, supposed to be as early as the third century 13. c. They represent domestic utensils, a loom, a horse, a landscape with houses, &c.—Academy. The bridge to be constructed over the Hawkerbury river, New South Wales, will be a remarkable work. This double track railway bridge will be 3,000 feet long, and the piers. according to the plans,. will require to be sunk about 170 feet in all below tiae. The estimated

cost is not less than $2,000,000. The Dutch State Raillvey authorities have been On- ducting experiments on the behaviour of different paints for ironwork. They have shown that red lead best re- sists the action of the atmosphere. It was found, also, that the coat holds better on iron plates cleaned by pickling than when the plates have been scraped or ' brushed. The trial sheets were pickled with hydrochloric acid, washed with warm water, dried, and oiled..while still warm. It was lately announced that:the Crown Prince of Prussia had discovered , among some old dOcuments in the Palace of Potsdam an overture composed by Frederick the Great. This piece has been played with the original instrumentation, and' is to be filled up for the modern orchestra and published shortly. The manu- script may prove to be that of the overture to "Ads and Galatea" written by the 'Prussian King, who was not only a practised flute-player, but composed an opera and a considerablemumber of shorter pieces. BRONZE INCRUSTATIONS.—ItI a recent article in the Cherniker Zeitung Professor Kaemmerer gives some in- teresting particulars of his researches into the nature of incrustations which form on bronze statues. In making an analysis, the-professor finds that the constituent ele- ments of bronze represent only a small percentage; the spots are formed in most cases by deposits of foreign ' bodies en the bronze by wind, smoke, rain, and more especially by' birds. After having tried in various ways to cleanse the surface of bronzes so speckled, he has found no dissolvent to answer so well as cyanuret of potassinm. In order to prevent the corrosion of the sub- jacent bronze, the period of contact i 8 limited, and the . bronze should'be well washed with water, immediately after-which it resumes its beauty and primitive lustre. PISCICULTURE IN FRANCE.—The report of the French National Acclimatisation Society states, amongst other • things, that much attention continues to be given to the stocking of Trench rivers with fish, and very encourag- ing accounts of what can be accomplished in this way have been received from several quarters. The society is observing with special interest all that is being done ' in this direction,,not only in France but abroad. Amongst . others whosre working, M. Rene Semall6, of the Puy-de- Dome, has•come to the conclusion that before attempt- ing to populate the rivers with the more choice and also, for the most part,- most voracious species of fish, it is de- sirable to secure for them an adequate food supply by , providing also abundance of fish which feed on plants. He has therefore placed a large quantity of young carp in the streams near his residence in the Puy-de-Dome. We observe that the National Fish Culture Association : has made arrangements for the importationi of a large consignment of carp from Gerniany for the waters of the United Kingdom. . AN AQUATIC E'xiserameNr IN THE Talauss.—The Lord • Mayor of London and a large company of fnavall and , military officials and others recently witnessed some ' experiments in the Thames at Westminster recently • from the decks of ,river steamers, while thousands of , other spectators 'crowded the embankment by the . Houses of Parliament or took a more distant view from , the bridges. Six or eight persons, clad in costumes of • ordinary appearance, and not one of them able;to swim, were found ready for a plunge into deep water on the simple assurance that their garments would keep them • from drowning, and they embarked in a small boat • whichirowed them into clear water. Then the tall figure of a woman, • impressively cheerful in attire, • rose suddenly in the boat, and, with a frantic wave . of her sunshade, tumbled overboard. Two of her fellow passengers, Who seemed_to be naval andmili- tary officers, threw - themselveg• into the water, to rescue her, which, • had she been sinking, they might , easily have done, although they know no more of swim- ming than herself, for, clothed as they were, they found • it impossible to sink. A sedate clergyman, seated in the • bows, became-so excited that he too lost his balance and splashed into the stream, while all the others, one by one, ,timidly followed until all were seen floating comfortably about with their heads just clear of the surface. Colonel , Clarke, RE., of the 'lnventions Exhibition and others • acquainted with•the secret, explained that clothing , worn by the adventurers was made of a fabric in which fine threads of cork were interwoven with wool, silk, or other material, and, without presenting any conspicuous peculiarity of appearance, rendered the wearer perfectly buoyant. Theunventor, Mr. Wm. Jackson, who is an exhibitor at Boathaensington, was introduced, and was much applaUded by the spectators for his successful experiments. AN Et ECIII.O-IinCHANICAL• CLOCE.—An.ingenious appli- cation of electrical power to the automatic winding of clocks has been invented by Mr. Chester H. Pond, an American gentleman, well known in scientific circles, particularly in the United States. In the ordinary clock the action is maintained by means of either a spring or a weight, the clock having to be wound up at stated periods, usually eight thy. In the electro-me- chanical clock powerful springi, heavy weights, and cumbrous gearing are dispensed with; hence the fric- tion is greatly reduced, and the clock requires no atten- tion whatever as regards winding. This operation is performed every hour by-means of a small electro-motor, which is fixed at the base, of the clockwork, and is con- nected with a small open circuit battery placed within the clock case. The elod,k is driven through a small flat coiled spring, to which a -slight initial tension is given when the clock -is made, and which -is kept at a uniform tension and acts directly on the hour wheel. This wheel, each hour-of its revolution switches the elec- tric current through the motor, which 'revolves rapidly for six seconds and Imparts a rotary motion-to the barrel on the centre arbor containing the clock spring. One revolution of this barrel puts the spring sufficiently in tension for running the ,clock one hour, at the end of which period the motor is again 'automatioelly started and the operation of winding-up repeated, the battery resting during the interval. The process is thus auto- matic and continuous from year to year, and the bat- tery is in use only six seconds every hour, or less than 15 hours in a year. The tottery, it is stated, will, in ordinary, last for two years, and can be replenished for a few pence and without interfering with the time of the clock; the first cost of the clock being, it is stated, considerably less than that -of an ordinary 'clock of the same class, notwithstanding its electrical accessories. A large number of clocks in a -building can be controlled and regulated by one main 'clock and 'battery. By a simple arrangement the ordinary service wire on a rail- t. way can bused -for giving an instantaneous and uni- form signal.rfor connection with every clock on the line, thus securing uniform time throughout All this was -demonstrated to us on a visit -to the office oflVlr. B. F. tWatkin, of 29, Leadenhall Buildings, London who states that these docks are already in sonsiderabie use in the United State—Times.

THE ELECTIoW -CAMPAIGN. Wilma& Mr. Tom Cottinetham Edwards-Moss has been selected as the Conservative candidate for Widnes Division. Warr Canenntit.—Mr. W. F. To! lemaehe, M.P. for West Cheshire, has announced that it is his intnition to retire, from political life, und that he will not again contest a con- stituency. Inn LATE Nunn/tn.—The Right Hon. W. R. Gladstone has expressed entire confidence In the result of the Midlo- thian election, and has withdrawn from the candidature of the Shipley Division of Bradford. MOCK ELEcriosts.—By way of educating the newly en- franchised agricultural labourers of Wiltshire to exercise the political right flow conferred upon them, and of proving the absolute secrecy of the ballot, meek elections have been held In different parts of the country. BELFAST.—The only section of Belfast which the National- ists have threatened is the West Division. On Saturday a deputation waited on Aid. J. H. Has' ett, J.P. (13onservative), of Belfast, and r( quested him to come forward as a candidate for the seat. Mr. Haslett consented. No Liheral candidate has been nominated MANCHESTER, Eater.—The Bight Hon. A. J. Balfour, M.P., commenced on Saturday his campaign as the Conser- vative candidate for East Manchester by addressing a crowded meeting in the Public Hall, Bradford. A reeoln- don pledging the meeting to secure the return of the right hon. gentleman was carried. Sir William Harcourt met the "Liberal 250" of Derby on Thursday evening, and received from them a vote of confidence. Sir William declared himself in favour of local option pure and simple, and said he had come to the con- clusion that the Constagious Diseases Acts ought to be re- pealed.

TEE APPEAL OF LOUIS RIEL.—The Lord Chancellor de- livered judgment on Thursday morning, at the Privy Coun- cil, Whitehall, in Rid's application for leave to appeal against his sentence of death, and said they had some to the conclusion that the application be not granted, and that the petition be dismissed. SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT AT DERBY.—Sir William Har• court, on Saturday, unveiled a statue ef the late Mr. M. T. Bass, erected by the people of Derby. Sir William went on to refer to Mr. Bass's efforts for abolishing imprisonment for delit, and Concluded by saying that he was a type of a member of Parliament that was unhappily becomina rare.

MR. CRILDRR AT ORTON PARK. On Saturday Mr. Childers addressed an openoair meeting of Liberals at Orton Park (the Dowager Marchioness of Huntiv'e), near Peter- borougb.—Mr. Childers, who was received with enthusias- tic cheers, said to carry on needed reforms would require that a strong Liberal Government should be placed in power if they were to be done efficiently. AN ADVERSE VOTE —On Saturday Mr. J. E. Gladstone, the Conservative candidate for the Span Valley Division, addressed the electors of the Liversedge district. The meeting was rather stormy throughout. When a resolu- tion was submitted declaring that Mr. J. E. Gladstone was a proper person to represent in Parliament that division it was lost by a majority of two to one. SIR VARNER HERscHELL ON Loup SALISBDRY.—Speak- Iag at Lindal-in-Furness on Saturday Sir F. Herschell said there was no man who had more bitterly opposed household suffrage than Lord Salisbury. In all the bills that had passed through the House of Lords he (Sir Fatter) had never known Lord Salisbury introduce anything that would make them more beneficial or Advantageous to the people. CHESHIRE LIBERAL CANDIDATES AND DISESTABLISH- MB/QT.—The Rev. Canon Cooper, vicar of Tarporley, has, by arrangement with the ecclesiastical authorities, addressed a letter couched in identical terms to the Liberal candidates - for the borough and county divisions of Cheshire, inquiring - into their views respecting the question of disestablishment. The uniform reply of all the Liberal candidates is that it is premature to raise the question, as it is not to come up for solution in the next Parliament. Mn. TREXELYAN AND TER CONDTTION OF IRELAND.—On Saturday, Mr. Trevelyam ME„, spoke at Taunton in con- nection with a testimonial presented to Lord Kilcoursie for his efforts on behalf of the Liberal cause at the last elec- tion. He said the most inconceivable statement of Lord Salisbury's was that the Crimes Act did not diminish out- rages. In 1881, before the Crimes Act was passed, there were 4,439 agrarian outrages; in 1883 there were only 762, and murders had decreased from 26 in 1881 to none in MU. WOMAN FRANCRIEB.—Of the candidates who are seeking election in November, the following have declared them- selves in favour of the principle of giving votes to women' who are owners or occupiers of property which would in- titles. man to vote :—ln England, 217 Liberals. 179 Con- servatives, 14 Labour candidates, 8 Independents, 1 Nationalist ; in Wales, 15 Liberals, 6 Conservatives, 1 Labour candidate, and 1 Independent; in Scotland, 27 Liberals, 14 Conservatives, and 1 Crofter. The figures for Ireland are not given. LORD GEO. HAMILTON AND Mn. CHAMBERLAIN.—Lord G. Hamilton, speaking at Old Southgate on Saturday, said Mr. Chamberlain had charged the Con lervatives with hold- ing office without power, ..ncl thus without honour, because , they had contrived satisfactorily PS-settle the difficulties and troubles of the late Government. The Treaty of Berlin bad secured the peace of Europe at a 'critical moment, and its violation must promote a disaster that could be averted only by the concerted action of the European Powers, and this

was rendered feasible by the friendly relations of the present G-vernment with foreign nations. Mg. BRADLAUGH AT MANCHIBTER.-011 Sunday after- noon Mr. Bradlaugh addressed a crowded audience in the Free Trade Hall, Manchester, upon The duty of Radicals at the forthcoming election." The Conservative of 1832 to 1887 was, he said, dying, and would have been dead bad he not been carefully nurseil by Sir Stafford Nerthcote, and the Conservatism represen‘ed by Sir R. Cross was as a prema- turely born baby that had the rickets. (Laughter.) As for Tory democrecy—(a voice: "A sham ")—no, it was not a sham, it was a sort of idiocy tempered with impudence: • a Bank of Elegance note that no political money- changer would give anything for; a sort of coin made of Woodstock pewter, silver-plated with Churchtllism. Mr. Bradlaugh then criticised Lord R. Churchill's receet address.

CHAMBERLAIN AND TRH BIRMINGHAM lINEM• PLOYED.—At a meeting of unemployed Birmingham opera- tives on Thursday morning, a letter was read from Mr. Chamberlain's secretary, in answer to the recent deputa- tions. Mr. Chamberlain says he has written to the Mayor, and that the latter does not see his way to open a special relief fund or become the treasurer. Mr. Chamberlain is of opinion that the reasons given by the Mayor are conclu- sive. It is important, he says, to ascertain the true facts with regard to the alleged want of employment in the town, and it is impossible that this inquiry can be properly oarried out except by the authorities specially charged with the care of the poor. Mr. Chamberlain has written to the Guardians in the hope that the Board may see the neces- sity for Such inquiry, and if necessary take effectual measures for the relief of any exceptional distress. LORD R. CHURCHILL,—On Monday night Lord Randolph Churchill spoke at King's Lynn. He disbelieved altogether that the great majority of the agricultural labourers would go solid for the Radical party at the elections. Speaking of the free education question, his lordship said that Mr. Cham- berlain, from intersabed motives and for a purpose which he had pretty accurately calculated, exaggerated the hardship which the payment of school fees entailed upon the popu- lation, and he also exaggerated the benefits which would be derived from the abolition of there school fees. Mr. Yonge took as his Cingng4.ornowa tilsoress )trilT etrtentat:blesso lookoattnteanneatoPet at the i''f'pe text verse 16, of the 6th chapter of St. Matthew, a more hopeful light, as the certainty of a rapid Oise "Let you light so shine before men, that they may the mind of a great burthen. see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." When, he said, George Peabody, the great American philanthropist, died in this coun- try in 1869, his remains, while on their way to America, were laid for a brief epos() within the walls of Westminster Abbey. He bad made himself famous England by his unrivalled munificence to the poor of London, and this temporary honour was deemed a fitting tribute to his distinguished work. On the site in the Abbey where his body was laid an ineerip- viola to Lie meuxery ha a been placed, and an its foot was the text he had just read, which embodied the Christian principle that animated and inspired his bountiful benevolence. The name of George Peabody would not be soon forgotten by the people of London, for in many a vast pile of dwellings for the working classes its memory was preserved. So did he give an illustration of the vast benefit that wealth can confer' upon the poor and needy if it was only animated by the spirit of Christianity, which was the spirit of humanity. He (Mr. Yonge) had adopted the text on that occasion as it seemed to him to have even a fuller illustration in the life and labours of that great nobleman who had just passed away. Those words undoubtedly expressed the aim which, ear- nestly cherished, and persistently followed, induced • the life of devotion to the good of men which Lord Shaftesbury lived. There was the Christian principle upon which he acted through the whole of his career. Lord Shaftesbury was a Christian, and be. he was a Christian he was a humanitarian. With him religion was more than a faith; it was more than a hope; it was more than a spring of personal consolation; it was even more with him than a rule of personal life.. With him religion was nothing less than an enthusiasm of humanity. Teach. lug him to love God, it taught aim to love his brother also, even the brother whom nobody cared for, whom everybody despised, and whom many even dared to oppress. Thus upheld Lord Shaftesbury from early manhood gave himself to a career of Chris- tian philanthropy such as has rarely been equalled in the history of the earth. While making a place for himself as the foremost philanthropist of his day there was to be found in him no single trace of vain-glory or of selfishness of motives or of desire for mere human applause. He did good from the simple love of doing good, from a deep sympathy with Christ's great purposes for men. Although he made large sacrifices during his long career, sacrifices of time and care, and effort and money, and even at one period of his history of the favour of his peers in social rank, he did it in the utmost symplieity, and with complete absence of ostentation. He was a brilliant instance of the humble Christian man in an exalted social station, spending and being spent for over 50 years in the services of his fellow-men. Although he was a Conservative in polities, he never showed any liking for mere party politics, and he abandoned the services of his party and embarked in that career of national and unselfish devotion in which he persisted through the whole of his lengthened life. Mr. Yonge next alluded in impressive and touching language to the condition of the poor people of this country at the time Lord Shaftesbury began his work of philan- thropy. In referring to the methods pursued by that nobleman to improve the condition of the poor, he mentioned that by means of the ragged schools, which Lord Shaftesbury was largely instrumental in de- veloping, 300,000 children had been taken from the streets, and turned into useful and industrious citi- zens. Lord Shaftesbury had been connected not only by name but by actual and personal work with nearly 300 philanthropic and religious institutions. In his concluding remarks, Mr. Yonge said it seemed to him that the working classes of this country, who owe so much to the labours of Lord Shaftesbury, might easily find one way in which they might imitate him and help to pursue the work for their own order which he so nolsly engaged in. He thought the working classes of all grades ehould resolve by all the power they possessed, and they had immense power, to further the libera- tion of all kinds of labour which was still in bondage. They could do it by Christian efforts, by the Christian efforts of earnest and persistent advocacy, by firm in- sistence upon the rights of men and the needs of the poor with all Parliamentary candidates. By untiring petition and agitation let them seek to further the cause of their own brethren. Working people should seek to help other working people who were still com- pelled to toil for hours longer than themselves and for wages that could hardly keep body and soul to- gether. Further, working people should be careful that, in seeking their own pleasures, they do not make 'busmen, cabmen, tram. car men, railway men, barmen, add barmaids work on both Sundays and week days for hours of exhausting and killing dura- tion. They should be careful also lest if by their de- mand for the cheapest clothing they compel women to work till late at night and at early dawn for star- vation prices. Did they not all need to become thoughtful of others, and to have a care lest in se • curing their own comforts they robbed another of his.

During :lc last week the Porte has made military preparation which c the first time appear to indicate an intention to march litc„ Reumelia. .4111.1111AD13, SUNDAY. At the latter place there are at present Zationed only the 7th and 13th regiments of infantry. d. BIMODAL. MONDAY.—Yesterday a battalion of volun- were whi h hay, been formed and equipped here, started for b_ • ',lamella amid general enthusiasm. PRILIPPOPOLIS, MoemAY.—The Government has given ders for levying the taxes et the province in kind, aed Lerge quantities of corn have thus been collected for the :Jai% The construction of fortifications at Sermon and Lwler points on the frontier continues, and measures have e7ell taken to protect the troops against inclement weather. The Bulgarian Government has I 7ce all in its power to avert such a calamity, but it is be- that Servia has gone too far to be able now to 'ecede. de SOFIA' • TUESDAY —The Prince of Bulgaria has issued a tree summoning all the National Militia to join the col- '?s, in order to be prepared for all contingencies. e.eYnA, TUESDAY.—Intelligence received here from Can- • anuounces that the Administrative Coarsen has passed tresolution in favour of union with Greece. The popula- L'eo, however, decline to take part in any insurrectionary ToYement against Turkish rule before Greece shall have `teetered war. Aruews, MONDAY.—Although the decree calling out three 'leases of reserves was only published on the 11th, 30,000 ittela have been enrolled. The excitement throughout the Provinces is unparalled since the revolutien of 1821. Thousands are arriving from all parts of the Pelopmesus, 11,altd the kegian Islands. Deleyannes, the premier, eulogised the deep t eelieg which the summons inspired, and added, "be aesured that the Government will strictly fulfil its duly lad combine your enthusiasm with the prudence which the 14agnitude of your threatened interest imposes on them." IMPLOMATIC REMONSTRANCE WITH SERVIA. BELGRADE, TnunsDAY.—At a meeting of the Diploma- t Body, held at the residence of the Italian Minister, it 'Pee unanimously decided to address a Note to the Servian Government with a view to arresting further steps on its Part PEIILIPPOPOLIS. TRURSDAY.—The news of the probability war between Bulgaria and Servia has caused the Turkish . Ihhabitants here to propose the formation of a volunteer Corns for service on the Servian frontier. No fresh intelli- price regarding the aspect of affairs has been received here ene any part of the frontier. rTHE BURMESE QUESTION.—THE BRITISH UL- TIMATIDL—IN TENDED DESPATCH OF TROOPS. CALCUTTA, SUNDAY.—A Rangoon correspondent tele- Valehed yesterday :—" Advines to.day from Mandalay state that great military preperations are being metae • there, every armed man available being called in. , Anarchy prevails in the country, and Mandalay is sur- rounded by bands of Dacoits, who are expected to attack tile towns." ALLARABAD,SUNDAY.—Much satisfaction has been created here by the announcement of the Government's ultimatum. It is thought that Thebaw will probably consent both to receiving the British Resident and to admitting the dispute between him and. the Association to arbitration, although his Ministers are said to be urging, an opposite Course. SIMLA, MONDAY.—The Indian Government is preparing to back up its ultimatum to King 1 hebaw by despatching additional troops to Rangoon. Should he resist its demands a force of 10,000 men will probably be required. The greater Part of these troops will be taken from Madras. It is feared that King Thebaw will massacre all the Europeans in his Capital unless they manage to escape on board the steamer Carrying the ultimatum. Since, TUESDAY.—The composition of the force to be despatched to Burmah in the event of such a measure becoming necessary is under consideration of the authori- ties. BOMBAY, TRURSDLY.—The Bombay Government has in- ',Red tenders for transports for the conveyance of the ex- peditionary force to BRIGLIII. The Press Association learns that the expeditionary force Of British and native soldiers to act against King Thebaw eirelll concentrate with as little delay as possible at Reugoon, "le contingents from Madras and Calcutta being timed to lrive there almost simultaneously. It is generally be- eeeved by the Indian military authorities that the duration "t the campaign, should it be necessary to take active ee_enerations, will be very short. 1110T8 BETWEEN HINDOOS AND MAHOMEDANS. NEW YORE, THURSDAY.—The editor of the Sun took the 'Chair at a meeting held here last evening for the purpose , (of raising a fund to aid Mr. Parnell at the approaching general election in Ireland. In the courre of the evening a ; cablegram was despatched to Mr. Parnell stating that a re- • Mittance of 10,000dols. was being forwarded to him. THE AFGHAN BOUNDARY QUESTION. TeturaArr SUNDAY.—Aecording to intelligence received her,i from Merv, the news of the amicable arrangement of tt Afghan boundary question between England and Russia has caused satiefactien among the Turcomans, who, how- ' :ver. are informed by the Russian officials that the question Of war is only postponed pending the construction of the tailway to Merv. A letter from Herat states that the Mglian Boundary Commission is encamped in the neigh- bourhood of Ghubran, with 1.000 mules and 1 300 camels. The daily expenditure for fodder for these animals is esti- mated at £230. TIFLIS, WEDNESDAY.—The Russian members of the e„Afghan Bounden, Commission left here last night. The Commission consists of Colonel Kublbeig, M. Lesser, seven topographers, two officers, the general staff, a paymaster, a anrgeon, and three interpreters. Twenty-seven sappers will be attached to the Commission, which will be escorted by a IlOtnia of Cossacks and a Turconean detachment. LORD SALISBURY AND THE TORTE. CONSTANTINOPLE, MONDAY.-10 conformity with in- attentions from Lord Salisbury, Sir William White has formally denied that the Prerniel'e references to the KAl- lern Question in his recent speech at Newport were in the east degree directed against the integrity of the Ottoman Rennin. THE EXPULSION OF AUSTRIAN SUBJECTS FROM PRUSSIA. VIENNA, SATURDAY.—In the Lower House of the Reichs- rath Count Taaffe replied to the interpellation recently brought forward by Dr. Von Grochelski in reference to the CaPulsion of Austrian subjects from Prussia. The Premier ' Stated that the Austrian Government immediately asked rrussia for explanations, and was informed that the Prus- eian Government regarded the expulsion fes a purely internal Measure, necessitated by the changes as regards the language and religious persuasion of the people. In view of the latteition taken up by th 3 Prussian Government in the matter a. reference by Austria to international law and commercial treaties offered no prospect of success, and the Govern- were therefore not in a position to take any fur- ther measures to obtain the withdrawal of the order for eetpulsion. Not only hal Paris not followed the reactionary tide et October 4th, but several departments which were on the mint of slipping from the Republic have now rallied to it. tAnother significant fact is that the 200 Conservatives may °a split up into some eighty avowed Bonaparrists and a like number of monarchists, while the remainder, al- though called Reactionaries, will not necessarily be anti- FRANCE AND TONQUIN. Smeerfin INTEnntfrriorr or A FUNERAL—The inter- ment of the remains of George Winters, who died from in- juries received at St. Helens Junction under circumstances reported in another paragraph, took place at Sutton church- yard, near St. Helens Junction, on Thursday afternoon. Al a mark of respect over 200 railway employes, representing the locomotive, traffic, permanent way, and sheeting depart- ments attended and walked from the deceased's residence in Junction-road, to the churchyard. A large concourse of spectators witnessed the procession, notwithstanding • the very inclement weather. The coffin was covered with wreaths —one of which had been forwarded by the members of the St. Helens Junction Cricket Club, of which the deceased had been an active member. An unfortunate accident marred the funeral ceremony. When the mourners and friends ar- rived at the churcliyard it was discovered that owing to the heavy rain the sides of the grave had given way, and the grave was partially filled. This caused a delay of about an hour—the relatives and sympathising friends spending the time in singing, scripture readings, &c., inside the church. The service was afterwards proceeded with without interruption. A party of gentlemen were talking about General Grant at Long Branch the other night, when one of them related the following, which the dead hero told —"Let: me tell you about the time I was at Long Branch. A gentleman said he had an B,ooodol. horse, and if I wanted to drive him I was welcome to do so. So one day I had him hitched up and started out. As I was going alone, I caught up with an old farmer, who was driving an ola 'plug' in front of a top buggy. The wind was blowing against him, too. Well, he just said glang, and I never saw so much dust fly in my life. Said I to myself, 'Grant, here you are sitting behind an 8,000 dol. horse and let an old fellow like that beat you." No ! no !' said I. I shook the reins over my steed, but, though he let himself out, I could not catch the farmer. I was covered with dust from head to foot and was a sad sight. 'Did the old farmer know you?' inquired the friend. Well, I didn't think he did; but hold on a minute. I caught almost up to him. The old fellow looked out of one side of his waggon and remarked—' General, how do you like the dust ? I think it's about time for a rain.' Well, I just clenched my teeth and said to myself, If this horse is worth 8,000 dol., I'm going to beat that farmer.' With one fine spurt I went past him, and as I did I exclaimed, 'My old friend, turn your buggy into a sprinkling cart. THE FXAMINER SATURDAY OCTOBER 24, 1885. GREAT LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN. SPEECHES BY MR. 11. GLADSTONE, M.P., MR. J. T. BRUNNER, MR. W. CROSFIELD. &c. The Liberal and Radical sentiment in Runcorn found adequate expression on Tuesday evening, when one of the most enthusiastic and successful political demonstrations held in the town for many years took place. The central figure in the proceed- ings was Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P. for Leeds, and so great was the desire to hear him that tickets numbering far beyond the capacity of the Public Hall, where the meeting was held, had to be dis- tributed. The meeting was timed to commence at seven o'clock, but two hours before that period people were crowding round the main entrance to the building. Shortly after six o'clock the Hall was filled to its utmost capacity. The long period of waiting was enlivened by the singing of Liberal songs, to the music of the Wesleyan Sunday School Brass Band, conducted by Mr. Tom Outhwaite. Mr. R. Moore gave the "Pilot of the State," the audience joining heartily in the chorus. A song entitled "Brunner and victory," composed for the occasion by Mr. W. Handley. was sung to the tune of "Wait till the clouds roll by," with great appreciation. One verse runs: Verdin won't do for our member. Bait's not enough. he'll see, Let it preserve" his faith, boys, Wider our creed must be. Salt, eoal, and lime need uniting In ehemloat mystery ; Brunner, be joins the three. bays. He shall our member be.

They all of them were hoping to have strength to do their duty whatever happened; they were thinking of the vote which they were about to give. It was to the Liberal party that the new electors of that district resident in Runcorn were indebted for the power of expressing their political opinion. (Hear, hear.) Prior to that great gift, the Liberal party had given them a great gift—the ballot, a gift by which they should be enabled to express their own opinions without fear of any kind. (Hear, hear.) The votes which were given prior to the enactment of the Ballot Act were given very frequently—be said it with due consi- deration—out of consideration for others rather than for the opinions of the voter. (Hear, hear.) That was now no -longer so, and every man could go to the ballot box and there deposit his own opinion about the candidate conse- quent upon the gift of the Ballot Act by the Liberal party. There was another great gift for which they were indebted to the Liberal party which had a great bearing on their present position. A leading organ of thought last Saturday uttered eentimente which he thought a great many people would agree with— that people were now fearing they would die of speeches. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) There Was a great deal to read, there Was a great deal to hear; there was very much to read which was worth reading, but there was a great deal uttered that was not worth listening to. 'I hey might apply that to the present company if they liked, although they were generally excapted—(laughter)—but to those who had to speak it was pleasant to think that the opinions that were expressed" were crystallised and embalmed in the public Press. They had every morning what seemed a day's work—they had the wisdom of the leaders of both parties, and they could judge for themselves. This was owing to the Liberal party. for had things been as the Conservatives would have had therm in times past they should hive no Press such as they had to-day. (Hear, hear.) And he would remind them that the special method which Mr. Gladstone adopted to pass the Act which freed the Press Was a blow at the prerogative of the House of Lords. The House of Lords, which they took to be the embodiment of the Conservative party. had stated that they would have none of it, and they rejected the ACC which was to free the Press. Mr. Gladstone, with that ingenuity for which they all thanked him, tacked the Act upon a money bill, and sent it up to the House of Lords, and they dare not touch it, and it was passed. (Hear, bear.) So much for the past; but the future Was of more importance to them. They were now about to use the franchise for the first time. In a Large gathering like that there were no doubt a great many differences of opinion. They were all Liberals—except one gentleman who appeared to have come into that hall as a Conservative, but he (Mr. Cresfield ) hoped that through the experience of the last quarter of an hour he had berm converted. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He was saying that they were all Liberals, but they were not all of one way of thinking. What he had to ask them that night was that so for as their coneciences would allow—and some people's consciences were elastic—they should put away all their private " fade" and they should all agree ever the great measures which the coming Parliament would be competent to deal with. (Hear, hear.) Lt order to do this they needed leaderehip, and he would re-echo the claim that they should give a loyal adhesion to the leader- ship of Mr. Gladstone (Cheers.) He would use words which he had heard spoken by Mr. Herbert Gladatone once when his health was proposed, coupled with/the House of Commons. He then Mid them of the trepidation with which he had looked forward to a candidature for Parliament, and the greater trepidation with which he had looked forward to' ' accepting the certain seat in Leeds, but he said he submitted his own judgment, which he was inclined to think was better than other people's, to his political lender. He (Mr. Crosfield) asked them to submit their rriwate opittions for the time being to their' political leader. (Hear, hear.' Some of them world say he did not go far enough for them. That might be, but he asked them to read Mr. Gladatone's manifesto, and if they read it in the light and spirit that he had he thought they would be convinced there was work enough for the next Parliament. (Hear, hear.) If it should not he so, let them do the work sketched in that manifest), and let them who wanted to go further remember what the good old book said, that if their opponent would not go with them two miles go with him one mile and then go on alone. (Hear, hear, and cheers) He would remind them that by the time they got to the end of the mile of Mr. Gladstone'e manifesto there would be plenty of people ready to walk with them the second mile. (Loud cheers.) Mr. W Summers, M.P., supported the resolution. Th working classes, he said, were now in the position of mas- ters, and if in the future they allowed statesmen to make blunders, they weuld have to bear the blame themselves. The next Parliament would be a national institution in sense in which no other Parliament had ben before. It would reflect the nation's opinion, and could any man doubt for a moment what the political complexion of that assem- bly would be. For his part he had confidence in his fellow countrymen; he believed them to be for the most part men who held rational opinions in politics as in other things, men, that was to say, holding Liberal and Radical opinions.. (Hear, hear.) He thought the prospects of the Liberal party were most favourable. He had recently been is Scotland, and the reports which reached him on every hand as to the political prospects of the Liberal party were most encouraging. (Hear, hear.) In political matters the county of Cheshire had had time reputation of being a ralier sleepy- place, and there were some who went SO far as to apply to the county the not very complimentary description of "mouldy." (Laughter.) He thought that they woeld change all that In the coming election. (Cheers.) Tne power was no longer in the hands of the squire and the parson ; It was in the hands of the people, and he believed that even from the" sleepy" county of Cheshire they should have a considerable contingent of Liberal members in the new Par- liament. (Loud cheers.) • ••

(dear. hear.) lie had had some I experience of election matters, and he knew that empty rooms and listlees audiences meant defeat, and that crowded . and enthusiastic audiences meant victory. (Hear, hear.) I He was sure their friend, Mr Brunner, could rely upon the I vote of every man present—(hear, hear)—and not only upon the vote of every man present, but upon their ability and , their energy to work and to get other voters. (Loud cheer- ing, and a voice: ‘• We'll begin now.") He way glad to know, at any rate, that there was one of their friends ready to set to work that night to do what he could for their frieed on his right; and be had no hesitation in asking them not only to support their friend there because of his personal merits, with which they were well acquainted, but because be was one of the army now advancing, marshalled, disci- plined, and is order to fight the battle which they meant soon to win. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) Mr Brunner, who was received with loud cheering and the singing of the song " Brunner and victory," then ad- dressed the meeting at considerable length. Their friend Mr. Oulton, he said, had told them that he had the heart of a.Cheshire man, and so he bad. (Hear, bear.) Born and bred within sight of the Mersey, he bad lived within sight of the Mersey all his life. There were men there, both be- fore him and behind him, and very much pleased he WAS to see their faces, who had known him to be a bard and con- eisteut worker in the Liberal cause for the last quarter of a century. (Hear, hear.) He was politically a true brother and meant to be of doe Chamberlain. (Cheers.) They had heard many a time and oft that evening of the manifesto of their great leader, and what tree Liberals and sound Radi- cals read in that manifesto—he confessed sometimes having to read between the lines. Mr. Gladstone had told them what he meant to aim at in the Immediate future. He did not condemn, and he (Mr. Brunner) trusted they would not condemn, a man who looked beyond Mr. Gladstone's im- mediate future. A man of his age might be permitted to look farther than a man of the reverent age and long service of their great leader. (Hear, hear.) The procedure of the House of Commons and the House of Lords was a dry sub- ject, but it was by no means an unimportant one. There were no less than seventeen distinct motions necessary to pees a popular bill through the House of Commons, and the results from that power was put into the hands of men like Ashrnead Bartlett, blockhead Warton, and spitfire Churchill —(loud groans)—who could render the carrying on of the business of the country utterly impossible. He asked them to support him in the amendment of the procedure of the House of Commons, because it would prevent ouch ecandals as they had seen in the last erosion. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Gladstone had called that a business meeting. He had attended meetings before in Runcorn that had been as enthusiastic, but when it was absolutely im- possible that the business could be done by them, but that night, after twenty-five years hard work for the Liberal party, he was proud and thankful to speak to tnern as voters. (Cheers.) That was a boeiness meeting for a real result would come from it. They had got their votes, and the question was what did they intend to do with them. (A voice: "Give them to you." Loud cheers.) He went a step further, and asked what did they want him to do with the power they would put into his hands. The new democracy looked with hope to the new Parliament for many a reform, but before any one of those reforms could be taken in hand they and he would have to seriously con- sider the Irish programme. Questions had been sent up to him which read as follow :—" Will you, if elected, vote for home government for Ireland—giving to 'the Irish people the power to manage their own affairs.? Will you use your best endeavours to place voluntary schools on an equal footing with board schools? Will you vote for a commis- sion to inquire into the present educational system? Would you, if e'ected, do away with religious teaching in schools ?" He was prepared to give a full and frank answer to every one of these questions. (Cheers) If elec- ted he should certainly vote for givieg to Ireland the power to manage Ireland's own affairs. (Cheers.) But what the defini ton of these words was to be be should not put into Mr. Parnell's hands. (A voice : "Never," and cheers.) He would not allow to any power in Ireland the right to put a duty on any English goods going there. (Hear, hear, and a voice ; " Parnell can carry that in spite of you; he will have sufficient followers with him." Cries of " Chuck him out " and disorder.) He was trying to answer the question in an honest fashion. With respect to voluntary schools, he was for fair play all round. Let voluntary schools put themselves on an equal footing with board schools if they could, and if they were not able to do so be could not help it. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) If anybody would show him aay good reason for a Com- mission to inqiiire irate the rather wide question of the pre- sent educational system, be should be glad to vote for it ; but he did not see the necessity of pulling up a plant to are if the roots were growing. (Laughter and cheers.) In an- swer to the question whether he would do away with reli- gious teaching in schools, be replied, in God's name, no. (Cheers.) t What was the reason of the discontent in Ire- land? Forty years ago there were eight millions of people in Ireland ; to-day there were five millions, and there was no more room for the five millions than there was for the eight millions. And why ? Because of absent landlords and unjust rents. In England rent meant what a tenant could afford to pay after he had recouped himself to:. his own skill and labour. But summer after summer the youth and manhood of Ireland came to this country, and worked bard and ate little in order to carry home money to pay what was called rent—(cries of shame)—not the amount that the an would produce, but the amount that could be wrung out of the affections of a man for his home. (Cries of shame an cheers.) Referring to local government, Mr. Brunner said that Mr. Goscben—(groans) —possibly the greatest authority on this question, had calculated that with a wise and com- mon sense arrangement in local sffaira, one third of the rates might be saved. To -leis (Mr. Brunner 's) mind th,y h*d three times too many collectors of rates, and three times too many rates (Hear, hear.) Ile laid very great stress on the advisability, nay the absolute necessity, of municipal life in our villages. He wished to have in every village a loci, council, which should manage the affairs of the village, and prevent any further encroachments on popular rights. (Cheers.) That when, as they found in Buncort,

the freeholders were entitled to the aurface of the ground, the lord of the manor should not tike away the minerals and the surface together. (Renewed cheers.) No more stealing of roadside stripe. (Beer, Istae) No more cloeing of paths across fields. (Hear, hear.) Speaking of the trammels of the feudal system that prevented landlor doing as their hearts dictated, Mr.'Bruoner. said be de- sired for England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales just and equal laws, except so far as was necessary to make them accord with national tradition. (Cheers.) To the Irish- men and Irishwomen in Runcorn and throUghout the length and breadth of the Island of Great Britain, he said for God's sake make not themselves foreigners and strangers amongst us. (Loud cheers.) Speaking of foreign policy, Mr. Brun- ner said a cardinal point in his- policy was the expulsion of the Turk from Europe. and he sated that Mr. Chamberlain ardently wished for his return as the Liberal member for the Northwich division. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner ex- plained the prejudicial operations of the law of primogeni- ture and entail, his illustrations being received with cries of shame, and asked if they would back hira in advocating the abolition of these laws. (Load cries of "yes.") The landlords had tied up freehold land se that it could not be seized in payment for debt, and he desired to enact on the behalf of those present, and on behalf of their poorer neighbours, tbat when a man had got a house full of furniture no power could take it away rom him by force. (Hear, bear.) The landlords had created settlement for them- selves, and he wished those present to help him in securing to the poor their household goods. (Cheers.) If they , would prevent the law breaking up a man's home, they would keep a man self-respectful and thrifty. Mr. Gladstone had done many a good work in the way of making his fellow countrymen thrifty; if he (Mr. Brunner) went one step further than Mr. Gladstone recommended, he asked them to support him as they had supported Mr. Gladstone up to that day. (A voice: "Oh, you are all right.") Answering a question sent up to him asking whether he would vote foe a Parliamentary inquiry into the circumstances which had induced the prosecution by the Treasury of Mr. Stead—(hear, hear,)—Mr. Booth and their assistants through whose labours the Criminal Law Amend- ment Act had been made anew, Mr. Brunner said he con- ' fessed himself bowed down with shame before them in that the men wbo had done what they thought in their hearts to be right should have been prosecuted—(cheers)—while the das- tards—the real criminals—were still allowed to hide in their dark places—(hear, hear); and if a Parliamentary inquiry could put that matter straight they might depend upon it that for a Parliatnentary inquiry he should vote. (Hear, hear.) He bad another question which was preceded by a statement of fact. "In Runcorn and many other places in this locality most of the public-houses and beerhouses are the property of brewers who tie their tenants to sell no other beer but theirs." (Loud laughter.) He (Mr. Brun- ner) could pity a man when he found it all " Greenall." The questioner aeked, "Are you in favour of legislation which woul4 prescribe brewers from being the owners of retail houses, so as to enable publicens to sell such qualities of beer as their customers prefer." (Laughter.) This was after all a very serious matter. He believed that these two points on which the magistrates had broken the law had brought upon us nine-tenths of the curse of drunkenness. (Hear, hear.) When they found that the magistrates in. stead of not granting a license to any man who did not keep his house open for the entertainment of man and beast, had given them here and there and everywhere to men who sold nothing but liquor—to mere temporary servants of brewers, instead of insisting upon the words of the law that each publican should be a man of substance, he thought they would agree with him that not only because a man liked two or three sorts of beer, but in the interests of sobriety, in the interests of those who would have all men honest, sober, and Gad-fearing this reform should be carried out. (Loud cheers.)

Mr. R Shaw moved "That this meeting recognising in John Tomlinson Brunner, Esq. a firm supporter of the Liberal party, hereby pledges itself to use every legitimate means to secure his return as member for the Northwich Division of the Contry of Chester." He confined his re- marks to the question of the extension of the franchise, and showed that Tories had been opposed to that measure of right and justice, offering to give a sovereign to a poor man who would bring him a resolution passed by the Conserva- tives of that constituency asking for the extension of the franchise. (Cheers ) He asked them not to be deceived about the education question. He believed the Tories were afraid of the poor man's child being educated, and were therefore raising the cry that the Liberals were going to do away with religion. Nothing of the kind. (Hear, bear.) The time was coming when the young people now in our schools would not be caj"led by false issues, but would be able to deal with these questions from knowledge, reading, and thought, and they would corns to the conclusion that this world was never founded, and all the machines of nature set to work, to make the rich man richer and the poor man poorer. (Cheers.) If they desired to do equal justice to all let them send Mr Brunner to Parliament that he might assist the Grand Old Man and the Liberal party to bring about this desirahle.object. (Cheers) Mr. W. Jepson seconded the m-tion in a vigorous speech, during which he was frequently cheered. Mr. Brunner, be said was not a pillar of salt. lie was a square man, and upon every aide of that square was the inscription, "Justice to all and oppression to none." (Cheers.) He Was in favour of justice to the Church; they would allow it to maintain itself—(cheers)—and place all on an equal footing at the grave and the wedding. (Cheers.) The poor man should not be trodden upon because he was a poor man, but they would give him the' privileges and the rights that he was entitled to by birth and citizenship. (Cheers.) Who were the men to carry out these things? (Shouts of "Brunner.") The men who had assisted them in times past were the men they must look to for the future—(cheerel —and he mentioned numerous and vital reforms passed by the Liberal party, advising those present to vote straight for Brunner. (Cheers.) Mr. J. R Frith supported the motion, and in a brief speech appealed to the ladies for their influence and support. The motion was carried unanimously. . _
Cheers hAving been given for Mr. Gladetone and Mr. Brunner, the meeting diversed.
THE OVERFLOW MEETING.

In conselnence of the Public Hall being en thronged by the enthusiastice numbers that attended, an overflow meet- ing was held in Bethesda School-room, and here also there were a large number present. The chair was occupied by Mr. S. C. Beckett, and speakers attended from the larger meeting.

The Chairman said that the chief object of that meeting W4ll to welcome Mr. Hobert Gladstone, the son of the man who for the past fifty years bad sacrificed his interest that he might benefit the people. (Applause.) Mr. Gladstone might well be called the" People's Will," and, be was sure, he would remain so up to the time of his death, which he hoped was far distint. (Applause.) The Chairman then announced that Mr. Herbert Gladstone had kindly pro- mised to address that meeting. (Applause.) • -

Mr. Kniveton, on being requested to speak, congratulated those present on the altered circumstances under which they were met. The last time the Liberals had a large public meeting in Runcorn things were differeat to what they now were. Then about one in seven of the men they met in the street had a vote. Now, thanks to the Liberal party, six out of seven bad that privilege—(applause)—and four out of the six were working-men. What was now the issue before the country. L rtterly they had had speeches from all sorts and conditions of men in all parts, and he was afraid that the issue had become somewhat obscured. Mr. Chamberlain was not, as some said, their leader. He was a grand man in the Liberal party—(applause)—but could afford to bide his time. At Scotland the other day Mr. Chamberlain said, "I have not come here to lay down a programme ; that is the work of an abler man than% Mr. Gladstone." (Applause.) He thus gave people to under- stand that he was a follower and not a leader. Neither was it a question of Lord Hartington, another able man in tlie ranks of the Lloeral party—for, unlike the Tories, they had many able men. They could find a dozen men who would be able to take the helm and steer the ship when Mr. Gladstone resigned his charge. There was great bother about disestablishment—a side issue. That was not the great question. It might, and probably would, come, if the Church party did not mind what they were doing. If Churchmen would honestly try to reform the abdees of the Church they might postpone disestablishment for an indefinite time, but if the English Church was not radically reformed from within disestablishment would effect it, and in a summary fashion. This was a utilitarian age, and people now loosed upon things from a practical standpoint. The real issue before the country was Mr. Gladstone's manifesto, The speaker then referred to various character- istics of that manifesto, speaking strongly in favour of the reform of Parliamentary procedure, fixity of tenure for far- mers, local government, and a reform of the House of Lords. Mr. Jephson, a working-man, in a short speech, said that the Literal party, which had passed so many beneficial measures, was the on, that they should support. The Tory party had ever been one of class legislation. They did not require that but something universalthatdiwvaiss its applicabili y tithe electors of that ion did theirn duty Mr. Brunner would be returned to Parliament. (At). olause.) He hoped that when the time came for them to disp-we of their votes they would boon the right side—that of progress ant Liberalism. (Applause.) Mr. Frith, who said that he had from boyhood taken an Interest in politics. reterrad to the Irish question. The Irish people, he said, had for generations had wrongs. He did not for a moment say anything in favour of boycotting, or the crimes that had be,n committed, bat thought that the wrongs of Ireland should he redressed. MrAilladstone had been willing to give redress, but frequent measures brought in by him had been thrown out by the House of Lords. He had been a Liberal all his life, and had voted for Likerals for above 30 years. Conservatism Ilerer did any good to the working-m rn and newer would do. (Applause.) If they returned Mr. Brutmer for the Northwicb Division they would send a true Liberal to Parliament to help Mr. Gladstone in carrying out those reform which he was deter- mined should be carried out. He trusted pit the men of Runcorn would help at the polling day to return Mr. Brun- ner with a good majority. (Applause.) Mr. Chilton (Liverpool) sad be believed that if they re- I turned Mr. Brunner he woulci make an t flizient representa- tive, and do good work for the country as a whole. Ile then referred to the semecy of the ballot to convince his bearers that they need have no misapprehension on that score. If anyone sought to intimidate them they had a thousand friends for one political opponent, and if it was In the power of that opponent t do a in man injury that man would have a multitude of friends who would do him far more good in return. He hoped they would work heartily for Mr. Brunner —(plause)—wilo was a good Liberal. If they were to compete with foreign nations the

- i working classes would have to be educated, and they /1268 t ' return men to Parliament like Mr. Brunner, who knew ' something of the effects of education on the continent, and was greatly in favour of extending our systt•m of educa- tion, so that it should be better in its character and more widely diffused. (Applause.) Mr. Yerwood asked Mr. Oulton would Mr. Brunner, if elected, vote for the " introduction el Bradlaugh " ? (Laughter.) • Mr. Oulton replied that he was not in a position to answer for Mr. Brunner, and the interrogator would have to torus his conclusions from what Mr. Brunner had from time $o , time said as to whether be would vote for Mr. Bradlaugh. ' He thought, however, that the Bradlaneh difficulty would not again arise ; the probability WAS that Mr. Bradlaugh, if returned, would simply take the oath as other members did. and pass on to his seat. Mr. Fletcher (Northwich) congratulated the people of Runcorn on the magnificent meeting in toe Public Hall. The element of personality had been baeished from the speeches. Some people would have them believe that the contest was one between a cask of soda and a pillar of salt —(laughter.)—but it was nothing of the sort. It was be- tween Tories, the opponents of popular liberty, and the Liberals, who sought the greatest happiness of the greatest number..., (Applause.) ___ _
Mr. E. 'P..Willis.ms (Northwich) also made a few re- marks.

Mr. Herbert Gladstone, who was received with cheer npon cheer, said that he came to Runcorn to help in a good caws.% He welcomed that meeting as showing the splendid prin- ciples of enthusiasm of the Liberals of Runcorn. He had come over to help in the good cause of Liberalism. (Ap- plause.) It was the duty of every man, if he had a moment to spare, to give help where it was wanted, and he was glad indeed to accede to the invitation he received to speak at Mr. Brunner's meeting. But he scarcely thought that Mr. Brunner wanted any help. He had plenty of friends, able speakers, to assist him, and with the aid, of the Liberals of Runcorn, Mr. Brunner would, he was sure, defeat the enemy. He was told that the Tory candidate was connected with the ealt industry. Ha presence in the House of Com- mons seemed to be particularly desired by the Conservatives, seeing that Lord Randolp:q Churchill had himself written a letter in his favour. There was very little salt among the Conservatives, and they wanted to gets little from the well- known salt district of Cheshire. (Laughter and applause.) But if they gave salt the Liberals could give pepper— (laug,hter)---ind they would prove that Cheshire no longer deserved the title of Tory. Cheshire hitherto had been sunk in the bed of hopeless Toryism, but now the prospects of the Liberal party in that county were very favourable. Mr. Gladstone then referred to Protecti6n, and said that if ' "
, . the people allowed the Tories to go back to that old system they, the working cases, would be the sufferers. In an-

_ . ewer to a questio;„ he adnaited that the late i.bral Govern. ment did tax the country to the twee of £lOO 000,000. The amount of money asked for by Mr. Childers was £94,000,000, and, as most knew, the Government did not only depend upon the tax,..tion of the country for its resources of revenue, and a sum of about £14,000,000 per annum was derivable from the poet and telegraph offices, and other sources of revenue. Therefore the proposed tax amounted to about £78;000.000. Conservative candidates endeavoured to gull the electors by saving that the hate Liberal Govern- ment proposed to pass a tax of £100.000,000 lie admitted that £78,000,000 was a high figure, but why was it 80 For one reason, because the Liberals had done their best, and not without effect, to pay their debts as they went along—(applause)—and they had never ceased their efforts for the reduction of the National Debt. (Renewed applause.) He would challenge comparison of taxation as between the Liberal Government of 1868, the Conservative Government . .

of 1874, and the Weral tiorernroent of 1880. The palm was was carried off by the first Liberal Government, and although they left the Conservative Government of 1874 a large surplus and a balasce of £7,000,000. the Conservative Government left the Liberals a deficit of £B,OOO 000, and a baloce of a little over £3,000,000. They were now hearing a great deal of this question from Conserva- tive candidates, but why had not they heard it before now, and could his questioner point to any one instance of a Conservative of note coming forward, either in the House of

Commons or on a public platform and denouncing the Gov- ernment for spendiug too mach money in any one particu- lar ? The main accugation of the Conserv-a:ices had been that the Liberals had not spent sufficient money. With regard to the proposed beer duty, Mr. 11. Gladstone said that the Liberals did not propose to raise the tax because beer was the poor mai,'s drink, but that the whole people of the country should bear their proper share of the burche, in view of an expected Russian war, and, at the same

time, taxation was proposed on the monied classes. (Ap. plause.) Mr. King proposed, and Mr. Williams seconded, a vote of confidence in the candidate, Mr. Brunner, pledging the meeting to use all legitimate means to secure his return. Mr. Brunner, before the resolution was put, made a short speech, in the course of which he said that he had voted a. good many times, and never vet on the winning side. He meant to vote this time not for Mr. Brunner, but for be Liberal cause, and he hoped that the result would be a different one. (Applause.) He worked for Mr. Gladstone in 1865, and the spirit that than animated him continued to animate him yet. (Applause.) The resolution, on being submitted to the meeting, was carried with applause, and the meeting then terminated.
