LIVING SIX YE &5 WITHOUT GOING TO BED. Mr. EDITOR,—WhiIe spending a few days at the pleaautt seaside town of Aberystwith, C .rniganshire, Wales. I heard related what seemed to nte either a fabttlous story or a mar- rellous cure.

The story vas that a poor sufferer who had not been able to lie down in bed for six long rears given up to die by all the Doctors, had been sneedity cured by some Patent Medicine. It was related with the more Implicit confidence from the thrum- stance. as was said. that the Vion. of Llanrystyd was familiar with the facts, and muld vouch for the truth of the report. Having a little eurheltv to knew 11,-,w such stories grow in travelling, I took the liberty while at the village of Llanrystyd to call upon the Pinar, the Rev. T.-Evans, and to inquire shell this wonderful cure. Though a total stranger to him, both he and hie wife most graciously entertained me in a half hour's con- versation. principally touching the case of Mr. Pugh, in which they seemed to take a deep and sympathelc interest, having been familiar with his sufferings, and now rejoiced in vhat seemed to them a most remarkable cure.

The vicar remarked that he presumed his name had been connected with the report from his having mentioned the case to Mr. John Thomas, a chemist, of Llanon. He said Mr. Pugh was formerly a re,ident of their parish, but was now living na the parish of Lianddeinol.

I never under- stood that my case was ever given no as hopeless by any phy- sician I have been tr«ated by several doctors hereabouts, as good as any in Wale., but unfortunately no prescription of theirs ever brought the desired relief.

Fifteen years ago, he said, I firs, beeame conscious of a sour and derange.' st •otsch and lofts of appetite, which the doctors 010 me was dy,pepsis. What food I ouuld hold in my et,•MaCh : seemed to no me no good, and WILB often thrown UP with painful retellings. lute was fo lowed af,er a time with hoarse.. nest, and a raw soreness of the throat which the doctors called bronchitis, and I was treated for that, hot with little success. Then came shortness'! breath and is sew, of suffocation, ee- peeiallypigh s, with clammy sweat, and I would have to getout of bed and sometimes 01)00 a door or window in wiltter weather to fill my lunzs with the coidair.

MY bowels were moved a. by a gentle cathartic, and I felt a sense of quiet comfort all through such as riled not befcre realised in many years. div.head: FHE EXAMINER.
div.p: FHE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 24, 1885.
MR. WILLIAM CROSFIELD'S Election Ad- dress as the Liberal candidate for the borough of Warrington will be found in flother column of this day's issue, and we

. Commend it to the attention of our numerous leaders—Conservative as well as Liberal. It ts a thoughtful and temperate production, 'Which, while conservative in spirit, reveals ,the ardent politician and the sound Liberal. 04. r. CRosEIELD is a reformer, but he is not revolutionary; and he believes in a policy that is constructive rather than obstructive. A.s a close observer of events, he has not for- Rotten that business in Parliament has been deliberately obstructed; he would therefore 'clear the way" in both Houses, and give the Lords to understand that they exist on !utterance ; they must behave- better in the tuture or they will be compelled to submit to 4 change in their constitution which will be ~..htere radical than will be agreeable to them. with regard to foreign affairs, Mr. CRoSFIELD dicates a line of action which, we doubt not, conservatives as well as Liberals will ap- Prove ; he would carefully protect the in- retests we have in every part of the world, Without encroaching on the rights of our , neighbours, He sees no need as to our colonies of departing from the policy which, ih the main, has guided both political par- ties ; he would maintain the unity of the empire whilst preserving and extending the Dtinciples of self-government. We are glad t° see that the Liberal candidate makes I:lecial reference to the government of llclia, and that he shows himself anxious `e maintain the good will of the subject races of our great Dependency. We in this country have a vast responsibility resting 'Pon us with the 250 millions of people corn- kitted to our care. It is a responsibility Zhich, we do not hesitate to say, Parliament s never sufficiently realised ; and there is IlPecial need in the House of Commons for like Mr. CROSFIELD, who wit strive to I '.° justice to India with a view to 'thnulating the loyalty, industry, and 1/rhsperity of her people. But whilst %king abroad, Mr. CROSFIELD is not ttlctglectful of those nearer home. He looks ,ei the new Parliament to deal with the hEihurnerous problems which concern the vhYsical and moral well-being of our town Pulation ; " and, ' if returned to St. , n3hen's, he will bring a wide experience of 1 t:tY life to assist in the rightful solution of 1 hI ese problems. It need hardly be said that I A goes as far as Lord 'SALISBURY in the i tVection of Local Option, and a little fur- He goes all the war.; for he expresses opinion that Licensingl .Reform "should hut stop short of a law giving to the ree- rsers the power to regulate the issue of pub- Ive,-house licenses.' Cardinal MANNING, "era addressing the inhabitants of Warring- in the Drill Hall the other week, was itz'rY earnest in urging the necessity of send- representatives to Parliament who were i. th avour of the popular veto ; • and it is not, :oerefore too much to say that his Eminence jo vlcl find in the Liberal candidate a man &this respect after his own heart. Lord 48..- ut(Y suggests that, under certain cir- %asta.nces, "the trade" should be compen- dis,e,cl ; but if questions of this kind are to be to Lussed, brewers should be the last persons a t o Parliament. Send t They have too much - stk tjo e to give a dispassionate opinion; it is be lAla e d appealing to the cat to say what should one M . with the cream. tipier; C.i<OSFIELD has great faith in the prin- oll t, .of local self-government ; and counts Itj "eh' early application throughout the three rigd'ms. He recognises the special claim

to consideration that Ireland possesses in the centuries of wrong from which she has suf- fered, and is, therefore, "in favour of grant- ing to the Sister Isle the greatest possible measure of self-government." A thorough reform of the Land Laws is with him a mat. ter of course; he does not. as is the case with Lord SALISBURY, confine himself to kicking against lawyers' bills. He would certainly simplify and cheapen transfer, but he would do more than that; .he would get rid of those infinitely greater obstacles which are involved in the barbarous system of entail and primogeniture. Trade has been set free, and when the land, too, is freed, it is not too much to say that, instead of " penury and woe," "health and plenty will cheer the labouring swain," while the dwellers in towns will be relieved of that grinding pressure of competition which makes the struggle for existence so terribly hard. Mr. CROSFIELD, as a practical politician, makes but brief reference to the question of Disestablishment ; he knows that so far as England is concerned there is no likelihood of the matter being dealt with by the next Parliament. It is otherwise as to the Scotch and Welsh Churches; and if Disestablish- ment be pressed by the people of Scotland and Wales, he will assist them in freeing themselves from the yoke of a minority, as the people of Ireland were freed. Touching the difficult question of Elementary Education, the Liberal candidate Lakes sides with Mr GLAnsToNE rather than Mr. CHAMBERLAIN He does not subscribe to the advanced views which we ourselves have expressed; but he shows himself anxious of relieving poor parents of humiliation in applying for school fees ; and he is " prepared to further an in- quiry having for its object the removal of such inequalities as exist between Volun- tary Schools and Board Schools." Mr. CROSFIELD is not blind to the tendency to the increase of the national expenditure; he observes that this tendency must be " strenu- ously opposed," but, as he truly remarks, individual members in a matter of this kind must have "the support of their constitu- ents." We want many mQte m,3mbers to join the PETER RYLANDS band of economists ; Lnd we venture to say that they will speedily he forthcoming if the electors make it known that there must be less pull at the purse- strings for Quixotic enterprises, whether in the Soudan or Afghanistan. In conclusion the Liberal candidate says:—" So far as it is necessary to attach myself to any one man, I desire to take my place athong those who follow our veteran leader, Mr. GLaiosToNE, as long as he is willing to place himself at the head of the party with whose so-opera- tion he has been enabled to confer so many benefits upon the nation at large." Mr. CROSFIELD'S address begins with a graceful reference to the retirement of Mr. McMrsl.- NIES, M.P., and it ends, as will be seen, with a not less graceful tribute to Mr. GLADSTONE. It is throughout in the right vein; it is clear exposition of principles; and is in every way worthy of the future member for War- rington.

The Liberals of Runcorn held a great meet- ing. and an overflow meeting, on Tuesday evening in support of the candidature of Mr. J. T. BRUNNER, the Liberal candidate for the Northwich Division of Cheshire. It is very gratifying to observe that the new electors are showing themselves thoroughly in earnest, and that, despite the sneers at their intelli- gence by such upstarts as Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, they are letting it be known that they have sense enough to see on which side their political bread is buttered. Mr. HER- BERT GLADSTONE was "the bright particular star" of the evening, and it is due to him to say that he shone with a brilliance worthy of his name, and worthy of the occasion. He did not make a long speech ; but it was full as an egg is of meat ; and it had a Radical ring with it which was heartily welcomed by the audience. The high and dry Tories who have been building castles in the air on the supposition that it would be possible to de- tach a number of moderate Liberals, because of the extreme views of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, must he grievously disappointed with such speeches as that of Mr. HERBERT GLAD- STONE. So far from giving the cold shoulder to the apostle of Radicalism, he shows him- self ready to work by his side. He rejoiced to think that the whole of the Liberal party ' were united in saying, with Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN, that taxation should be equally distribu- ted between rich and poor ; and he pointed out that the DEAN of WELLS, , after making due inquiry, had come to the conclusion to " advise Churchmen to accept Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S views on Free Education" As to the third point— compulsory purchase of land for allotments and small holdings—he thought it would not be long before the Liberal party as a whole would accept that also Mr. GLADSTONE was pleasantly ironical with those of the Church party who will insist on raising the question of the Disestablishment of the Eng- lish Church, notwithstanding that it is dis- tinctly understood amongst Liberals that the next Parliament will have plenty to do with- out dealing with Disestablishment. Their attitude reminded him of the little incident in "Box and Cox," where Box says to Cox— Can you fight? When Cox says "no," the bellicose Box valiantly exclaims—" Come on, then!" The audience enjoyed this sally immensely. as they. did the satirical allusion to the tiger shooting of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, the politician who had come home from India with the spirit of the tiger which he shot at but failed to hit. He offered his Lordship a bitter pill to swallow when, in 1 contrast to such smooth words as "our Irish brethren," now used by the Member for Woodstock, he reminded the audience that so late as last year Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL spoke of the followers of Mr. PARNELL as " that legion of foul fiends." We have had occasion in these columns to point out the shameless political immorality of his lordship, and we put it to Irishmen who may read his plausible speeches whether they can in the future trust the Jim Crow of politics who has, in the most unmeasured terms. abused them in the past. Following Mr. GLADSTONE, Mr. BRUNNER made a forcible speech, in which he showed that, while he is loyal to the ex- remier as the leader of the Liberal party, he is in strong sympathy with the advanced view so ably advocated by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. The new voters, he said, were looking with hope to the new Parliament, and those who know Mr. BRUN NZR—and there are few Liberals in the Northwhich Division who are not by this acquainted with him—will have no hesitation in saying that they can depend upon him at all times to stand by the cause of the people. He is not of the easy-going order of poli- deans who are disposed to "rest and bc thankful" with the enfranchisement of th( masses. He rightly regards the suffrage a( the means to an end, and will not be content whether in or out of Parliament, until he
IJ

has " foiled full many fallacies and routed many wrongs." But the Liberals of the Northwich Division must insist that it shall be in Parliament that his work shall be done The people are with him; the people now have votes ; and if there is good organisation and hard work " BRUNNER and victory" will, before many weeks are over, be a delight- ful reality.

The Campaign in the Newton Division is getting lively. Each candidate has this week published a formal Address to the Electors That issued by Colonel McCoRQuoDALE, the Liberal candidate, will be found in our ad- vertising columns ; and it will be seen that the Colonel shows himself to be a devoted follower of Mr. GLA.DSTONE. Already there have been several enthusiastic meetings in support of the Liberal candidate. The new voters in the Division are seen to be alive to the opportunity which is before them—a cir- cumstance which would appear to have come to the ears of Sir RICHARD CROSS, for he is now letting it be seen that he is not a little anxious as to the result of the contest. He would seem to have a curious notion of the itness of things, and as to what is of interest to the electors ; he is a Home Secretary, and yet he is continually harping on foreign affairs. It is an old Tory trick, and was good for making "the groundlings " gape when they had no votes to give; but now that they are within the pale of the Constitution we are inclined to think they will not be put off with such a stale device. Sir RICHARD. speaking at the Tory demonstration in War- rington, on Wednesday, confessed that in the j storm of words they were getting " a little! bit confused with one and the other." Pos- sibly, and this may account for the travesty of history which he has given as to affairs at' home and abroad. He has the hardihood to ; assert that the late Government fell "simply because its own supporters did not give any further support to it." Does not this look very much like t hat Sir STAFFORD NORTH- COTE would call "a thumping lie" when placed side by side with the fact that, when the late Government were defeated for the first time on an issue of moment, so far from not having any support they ' mustered on the division no less than 25z against 264 of Tories. Parnellites. and Pub- licans. The Home Secretary goes on to say that "they slunk out of 'office "—a statement which is a libel upon statesmen compared with whom Sir RICHARD CROSS is a thing of shreds and patches." Whoever slunk out, it is well-known who crawled in, and that, too, after failing to exact pledges from the Liberals the obtainment of which, 'it was said, was essential to their taking office. It was a " patriotism " which was surely "a little bit confused," which led them to eat their own Words in order to ob- tain place without power, and which has kept them at the same work ever since. When in opposition, the Tories denounced the pru- dent arrangements which Mr. GLADSTONE proposed to make with Russia as "a base and cowardly surrender ;" but did they drive 'another way when they gc t the reins in their hands? Nothing of the kind ; they moun- ted the box near the end of the journey, and are now disposed to shout—" We've done it, and a very good thing it is." Sir RICHARD CROSS tells us that difficulties disappeared as if "by magic" when the Tories came into office. " It wassomething," he says, "like the clouds which they saw in mountainous coun- tries, and which looked very threatening and dangerous, but were suddenly carried away, and in the same way when the change of Government took place these clouds at once disappeared." Yes, and to carry the com- parison to a logical issue—which is too much to expect from a Home Secretary, who is "a little bit confused "—the present Gov- ! I ernment had just about as much to do with the disappearance of the difficulties as the trav- eller has with the clouds which are carried away in a mountainous country. The work for which the Government take credit was ;done to their hands ; while the jobs for which they alone are responsible are turn• ing out badly. There is the Berlin ' Treaty which has not brought peace, and - is being dishonoured; and what about " calm- ing the susceptibilities of foreign nations," when Lord SALISBURY has had to send a ; special message to the SULTAN to explain ' away his Newport speech? As for "the concert of Europe," there is at present a great deal more discord than harmony, and, as things go, there is every likelihood, if the Tories remain in power, of its ending in the performers breaking their instruments on each other's heads. The HOME SECRETARY, as a second fiddler in the band, is sadly' out of it;" he shouldn't meddle with what is foreign to him, or if he will strike in he ; should do so when there is less necessity for confessing that he is " a little bit con- fused."

THE REIGN OF TERROR AT CREWE.-011 the 14th inst. a memorial was sent on behalf of the Crewe Liberal Association to the directors of the. London' and North-Western Railway Co., making certain representations with regard to the alleged political intimidation at the Crewe railway works, and asking the directors to "issue a simple declaration that the men shall henceforth be perfectly free to exercise their franchise, both in municipal and Parliamen- tary affairs, according to their conscientious convic- tions." The secretary to the railway company has replied, stating that the memorial has been under the consideration of the directors, and he is in- structed to inform the memorialists that "the allegations contained in the memorial, which are substantially the same and of the same character as those which have recently appeared in the public prints, have already been inquired into, and the directors have satisfied themselves that the state- ments made in the memorial are without founda- tion, and that the men have always been perfectly free to vote as they please." Fenno'. BOARD —The monthly meeting of the Prescot School Board was held on Monday evening. Present Messrs. W. L. Evans (chairman), C. Spenceley, W. Golds - worth, J. T. Hall, T. P. Hewitt, and H. Cross(clerk).O the recommendation of the sub-committee appointed to consider the appointment of head school mistress for the infants' school, Miss E. Oldfield was appointed at a salary of £5O per annum and excess over £2O of the amount earned as government grant.—Mr. Hall drew attention to the fact that the fees for the present month were £4 3s lid, whilst the average attendance was more than in the corresponding period of last year, when the fees amounted to a greater sum.—Tne Chairman remarked that the poverty of Presoot was much greater now than it had ever been before.—mr. Spenceley thought it was a question of arreare.—lt wag ultimsteiy decided that the school master and school Milt. tress should submit to the committoe each month a state. ment of the arrears, remittances, &c.—Mr. Goldeworth said he thought teachers should not have the responsibility of writing off arrears without the sanction of the Board. The monthly return of attend Mee' and fees was received, but it presented no features of special interest. Lpun HARTINOTON AT GREAT GRIMSBY.—The Marquis of Hartington on Wednesday visited Great Grimsby to open a new Liberal Club which has been erected in the Market- place. At a banquet in the afternoon, Lord Hartingten said Conservative • pe cbes gen:rally contained something about the bribe offered to the agricultural labourers, which might he summed up in the expression " three acres snd a cow." tie (Lord Harrington) believed Liberal candidates would be able to contradict the allegation that they had ever thought of talking such nonsense. He hoped all Liberal candidates would confine their promises within bounds which were not only desirable but practicable. He hoped no one would take up extre.ne views in order to attempt to catch the votes of any portion of the newellectors. He asked for the same fairness on the part of their opponents. go hoped the new electors would place themselves confidently and firmly under the protection of the .Ballot Act, and exer- cise their new franchise freely and without fear. In the evening Lord Hartington addressed a croe.ded meeting which was held in the Prince of Wales Theatre. The funeral took place yesterday morning, and there was a solemn and imposing display of regard and esteem for the memory of the deceased gentleman. The proces- sion, which departed from Linden Lodge at eleven o'clock. repressnied all classes and conditions, and numbered no less , than 300 persons—a significant tribute to the position the deceased had occupied in the hearts of his fellow-towns- men. Numerous spectators lilac assembled along G reen way- road and in the cemetery, n‘ twithstanding the very inclem- ent state of the weather, and there were indications of mourning on every hand in the town. The procession was beaded by' Dr MacDougall (the deceased's medical adviser), the Revs G Wood, T Hackett, A P Watson (Weslevans), J D Thomas (Congregational), E Williams (Presbyterian ), William Preston M.A. tEstablished), T M Armson (Estab- lished), and Mr George Bellamy. - --WATRINGFON BOROUGEI POLICE COTiRT: MotenlY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Pickmere, and Mr. John Fairclougk. NEDLECT or FAMILY.—George Jones was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and family, who became chargeable to the Union on the 14th October. Prisoner's wife, Mr. Shearer, relieving officer, said, applied for relief on the day named, and from inquiries made it was ascer- tained that the man was working at Oldham and was earn- ing 22s a week ; he bad sent 18s in four weeks for the maintenance of his wife and three children. Prisoner said he was not earning so much as had been stated.—Hs pro- mised to look properly after his family, and the case was adjourned to see if he did so. Dausaexteess.—The following were dealt with for this offence :—Edward Griffin, in Sankey-etreet, Michael Daffy, In Hill-street, Morris O'Brien and William Healy, in Bank- street, each fined 5s and costs ; and Patrick Macdonald, in Sankey-street, fined lOs and coats. A DESERTER.— John Rearden, a deserter from H.M. South Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Orford Barracks, was handed over to tee military authorities. DRUTIDC ON LICENSED PREMISES.—WiIIiam Bowen was charged with being drunk on the licensed premises, the Fox Inn, Buttermareet-strmt, on Suuday evening, and with re- fusieg to leave when riquested. He went to the house whilst drunk, coed disgusting language to the landlady, Mrs. Saxon, and had to be ejected by a police-constable.— He was fined 101 and costs, or, in default of payment, 14 days' imprisonment HiGnevae ROBBERY.—Eiward Turner was charged with being concerned in a highway robbery with violence at Rinver, in Staffordshire. Information was received by the police at Warrington to the effect that three men were " wanted " for the offence named, and prisoner, who answered the description of one of the men, was arrested by Inspector Berry. Prisoner was then at the holies of his brother in Prieetly-street. In answer to the charge, he said, "If you nlll speak the truth I do not care; I shall be all right."—Prisoner, who has lost an arm, was remanded to be dealt with by the }Oliver police. DRONKENNESS.—Mary Towey was sent to prison for a month for being diunk and disorderly in Cockhedge-lane on the previous evening. Annie Williams, charged with being drunk in Crown-street, was dismissed on promising to leave the town.

DIII7I,IKENNESS.—Bridget Donoghue, a young woman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttets market-street, and was ordered to pay 225, fins and costs. RUGBY RULES. LONGFORD EXCELSIORS V Sr. PAUL'S:A match was played between the above clubs on Saturday on the around of the former, which ended in a draw. Score : Excelsior, 1 minor point; St. Paul's, nil. WARRINGTON ROVERS V. FAIRFIELD WANDERERS.—A match was played on Saturday, on the ground of the for- mer, and after a very pleasant game resulted in a decisive victory for the Rovers by eight tries and three minor points to one minor point.

-- RUNCORN NEWTOWN WHITB STAR V. HALTON WHITS STAR.—This match was played on the ground of the latter, and ended in an easy win for Newtown by 1 goal, 6 tries, 15 minor points to nil. Whalley dropped a splendid goal. The tries were obtained by Cross (2), Fletcher (1), Heath (1), Whalley (1), and Owen (1). LIVERPOOL OLD BOIS V. RuNcourr.—Played at Run- corn on Saturday, when a very large number of spectaroro watched a magnidcent game, which was played throughout in good spirit. Runcorn started the ball, the play locating in the Old Boys' quarter. Cox nicolv frustrated Draper in makirg his return, and soon after Speakman was called upon to st-rp a forward effort on the part of the Old Boys, the Runcorn men pulling themselves togother, when Joule and Gatley got the ball close to the line, where H. Hughes got over Woods kicking a capital gool from the place. Fol- lowing this, hard play ensued in the centre, when the Old Boys were forced tc touchdown. Broady and Johnson fre-

quently appeared dangerous, but they were successfully tackled by Draper and Jones. After crossing over, F. H. Chambers starred the ball, which was, however, soon trans- ferred to the Old Boys' quarters, the Runcorn forwards playing grandly together. but the visitors were successful in keeping thorn off. Broady made a good attempt to drop a goal, Draper touching down. A raid was now made on the home line, but Wood tackled in fine style, stopping Cham- bers in a well-meant attempt to score, but up to call of time nothing but touchdowns were conceded by either side, the score being—Runcorn. one goal and three touchdowns to one touchdown. H. Hughes was very noticeaole by his dashing play. EARLESTOWN V. BLACKBURN ROVERS.—A strong team of the Blackburn Rovers vislied Earlestown on Saturday after- noon and met the holders of the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup on the M-snes. There was a large atten- dance of spectators, who witnessed a splendidly contested game. Unfortunately the home team could not muster their full strength. the absent players being Duxbury, Rich, and Ellison. the Ravers won the toss and chose to play down hill during the first half. Dagnall started the leather for the home team but the visitors quickly Assumed the aggressive, and in sjfew minutes notched their first goal from a scrimmage, and Rcrlton added a second goal a short time afterwards. The play of the home team was subsequently of a better character, but Walton was able to score a third goal for the Blackburnians. The remairder of the play in the first half was much more even and exciting, and amidst loud cheers Holcroft scared for Earlestown. Before half time the visitors added a fourth point. On the change of ends the Liverpool cup holders redoubled their exertions, and ,for some minutes severely pressed their opponents. After abont quarter of an hour's play Dagnall sent in a splendid shot, and as Woolfall attempted to stop it he was charged through the goal by Sims, and amid loud cheers Earlestown scored a second goal. Though the home team had the best of the play which followed, they were unable to score any additional points, and the Rovers were victori- ous by four goals to two. Teams :—Blackburn Hovers. A. Woolfall, goal ; F. horrock and Chadwick, backs ; P. R. Barton, Fletcher, and Whittaker, half backs ; N. Walton and Rushton, right wing ; C. Emmett, centre ; R. Blenkhorn and R. Roberts, left wing. Earles- town : J. Appleton, goal; R. Green and J. Green, backs' R. Bowker. J. Duxbury, and W. Lane, half bache ; H. Hot- croft and T Fergusoc, right wing; A. W. Dagnall, centre' J. W. Sims and J. Ogden, left wing.

div.p: NOTES BY. THE WAY.

That famous vorkshire club, Bradford, has again visited Lancashire, this time opposing Swinton. Same idea of the interest shown in the game may be gathered from the fact that it w-s witnessed by something like 10.000 spectators, who were treated to a grand game. The result was a draw ; Bradtord one try and four minors to Swinton one try and two minors. Broughton took a trip to Batley to oppose the cup holders and, although the weather was not propitious, a good and fast pate was the result. The Griffins proved the victors, but it was a narrow shave, the try of Batley being a poster. Result, Broughton one goal and one minor, Batley one try and nine minors.

Liverpool received a visit from Manchester, both sides being strongly represented, and, as was expected, a hard and pleasant game resulted. At call of time Liverpool were the conquerors by two goals to one goal, one try, and one minor.

Broughton Rangers lowered the celoure of Barrow, the game being played at Lower Broughton. Neither team had their full strength, Barrow in this respect having the advan- tage. Rangers one goal, one try, and four minors, to Barrow One goat and one minor. Warrington had for their antagonists Walkden, this team coming with a good rPpntal.ion, not having lost a game for three years. Abmt 2 000 persons witnessed a pleasant but very hard game. Warrington eventually won by one try and one minor to two minors.

A. splendid game was witnessed at Runcorn between that club and the Liverpool Old Bnys, the greatest interest being shown in the game, which ended in a win for Runcorn by one goal and three minors to one minor. Widnes met Birch on the ground of the latter, and, con- trary to expectation, the game ended in a draw. Birch second should have turned up at Widnes, but failed. This is now the second time Widnes have been disappointed. Widnes will be waxing wroth. . . . . .

St. Helens went as-far as Blackrod, but were severely thrashed by the collier men, having one goal, four tries, and two minors to nil scored against them. This is not last year's form for St. Helens. The Newton ground was the scene of a struggle on Satur- day last, the greatest rivalry existing between the Newton and Villein clubs, and after a fast and excitinet gam. New- ton were declared the winners by one try and five minors to nil.

Three men who were working in the recovery-furnace room were knocked down and also in- jured. Their names are Charles Wilson, who was struck on the head and severely cut; Luke Gregson, cut and bruised about the leg; and John Croft, injured about one of his ankles. William Travis, who had his leg broken, remained in the stores room at the works all night, and on the re- 'commendation of Dr. J. W. Watkins was conveyed to his home in a cab at eight o'clock this morning. The body of Byrne still lies at the works awaiting the inquest. At seven o'clock this morning a gang of about 80 men were set to work to attempt the recovery of Fleming's body. Their efforts were directed by the energetic foreman, Mr. John Bryce, but up to the present they have not been re- warded with success. The work is necessarily very slow owing to the immense heap of debris; but the men work heartily and zealously. Pieces of iron, brick, slates, wood, and straw were thrown over the entire works. A bale of straw was hurled a distance of 40 yards over two buildings. A redeeming feature of the catastrophe is the fact that nearly all the workpeople in the demolished buildings had left—in some cases only a few seconds before the explosion. 'The cause of the explosion is at present shrouded in mys- tery. It is not known whether or not the buildings are in- sured, but the damage to property cannot be estimated for some time.

TERRIBLE BOILER EXPLOSION AT NBWTON. TWO KILLED AND 12 INJURED. —GREAT DESTRUCTION OF PROPERTY. The village of Newton was thrown into conster- nation on Thursday night, when at ten minutes to six &clock a tremendous report, accompanied by a tremble jf cottage property, startled the inhabi- tants. The report was followed by a rumble as of falling bricks or other heavy material, described by one who beard it as like "a roll of thunder," and as the alarmed people, rushed to the doors of their homes they received an explanation which spread "like wildfire," that a disastrous explosion, result- ing in loss of life, had occurred at the extensive and. well-known Newton Paper Mills, owned and worked by Messrs. Gillespie and Mason. A crowd at once flocked in that direction, and their worst fears, were unhappily, realised. The anxious throng round the mill gates eagerly appealed to the work- men as they left the building for information as to the disaster and its consequences—and the an- nouncements that there were both dead and injured excited a painfully sad feeling. The news of the explosion rapidly spread to Earlestown and sur- rounding villages, and a gloom was cast over the entire neighbourhood. Newton Paper Mill consists of an extensive block or series of buildings to the south of Newton Bridge Station, and the entrance gates are fixed in Mill- lane or Warrington-road. Messrs. Gillespie and Mason, as the owners, carry on business as paper manufacturers, and find employment for a consider- able number of people resident in Newton, Earles- town, Golborne, Lawton, and intermediate places. The explosion occurred in what is known as the revolver. room," a department in which theoperations attendant upon straw, grass, and jute boiling is carried on. This depart- ment occupied a large two-storied building in the centre of the works, and found occupation for about half a dozen men. On one side it was bounded by what is known as the " poacher-room," on another by the grass and etraw room, on a third side by the " recovery-room," while on the fourth side are the stem boilers—six in number—which supplied motive power to the machinery throughout the entire works. The "revolver-room " takes its name from the revolving boilers in which straw, hay, and jute are boiled preparatory to undergoing pulping operations. These re- volving boilers occupied the ground floor, and there were two for boiling straw, two bay pans or boilers, and one for jute. The men who attended to them worked in a room above, and one men was appointed to each machine. LATEST PARTICULARS. _ NEWTON, FRIDAY FORENOON.

The terrible effects of the disastrous explosion at 'Newton Paper Mill were painfully evident this morning at day- bre.k. An inspection revealed the fact that the destruc- tion had been very much greater than was last night sup- posed, and it will take many months before the damago can be repaired. The "revolver-room " is a complete wreck— the only thing remaining upright being one of the five boilers which were in the room. This is surrounded by an immense heap of bricks, it'Oß machinery, smashed boilers, slates, and lumps of wood, while on every side are half de- molished and roofless buildings. It is supposed that when the straw-boiler exploded, the full force expended itself on the next straw-boiler, causing that also to explode, and this accounts for the severity of the des- truction. Heavy portions of the boilers flew on every hand, scattering'destruction in their path. One piece car- ried away a portion of one side of the jute and straw room —l5 yards away and inextricably embedded itself amen tat the machinery in that building while another por- tion crashed through the side of the " recovery-furoace " room, leaving only one half of the roof. A third lump of iron flew with terrific force against the steam boiler sheds, and they were partially demolished, and other sheets of iron were sent on the roofs and against the sides of other buieltriva. For a circle of at least 20 yards round where the " revolver-house " stood, ruin and wreck only re- mains. The fact that there were only two deaths seems almost providential considering the large number of persons placed in danger. There cannot be the least doubt from the wrecked and demolished buildings that bad the boiler ex- ploded a few minutes earlier a greater loss of life would have had to be !coned. It has been ascertained that instead of only six persons having been injured the number is at least twelve, and some of these had almost miraculous escapes. Besides the five men employed in the holler room, there were other time persons therein at the time of the explosion. One of these, a man named Louis .Boardman, was speaking to the dec,ased man Ilyroe, and while the latter was instantaneously killed Boardman escaped with serious scalds and an injury to his back. When Byrne's body seas discovered it was seen that an ionnensebeam had alighted on his bead, while his body was frightfully mangled—one ankle being smashed. Though his body was found last night, some portions of his remains were not picked up until this morning. Arthur Rawlinson, a youth was also in the

The Recorder of Sheffio:d,on Thursday, Passed sentence of six months' imprisonment on Itlnk9 Storey, a bankrupt tailor found guilty of fraud upon his creditors.
GENERAL NEWS.

Mr. W. B. Forster, M.P., is recovering from a slight re- lapse, but is unable to attend to business. In Palermo province, on Monday, there were 44 cholera oases and 21 deaths. In Spain there were 53 cases and 42 deaths. KAY'S COMPOWND, far Coughs and Colds, is equally service- able for Horses and Cattle. 91d, Is lid, and 2e Dol. —lldet. Mr. Mitchell Henry, M.P., has been adopted as the Liberal candidate for the Blackfriars and Hutchesontown Division of Glasgow. The Bath Corporation are going to further develop the mineral water bath at a cost of £20,000. The new buildings will be erected on the Continental system. On Saturday evening a lad was hammering a ship's rocket in the street at Walton, Liverpool, when the rocket exploded, injuring the lad, a woman, and six boys and girls. News from Copenhagen states that serious riots have oc- curred there, directed against the King and Government. The garrison has been reinforced, further disturbances be- ing feared. The British steamer Greyhound, Captain Hyden, has put back to Hong Kong to avoid capture. She had been plun- dered by pirates, the captain killed, and the second officer and chief engineer wounded. The Archbishop of Canterbury, in his charge to the clergy of Kent at Canterbury, on Wednesday, said it was a first duty to maintain the voluntary schools, and never, if possible, to transfer them. Three persons have been killed and five injured by a rail- way collision on a New Hampshire Railway. Five emi- grants have also been killed and a number injured by a railway collieon near Jersey city. A man named Smith attempted Is murder his wife and another woman at Hatton Le Hole, in the county of Dur- ham, on Monday, by cutting their throats. Both women are in a dangerous state. Smith has fled. Several of the leading farmers of East-Kent are killing their own sheep and sending the meat into the towns. They are selling prime joints of mutton at 84 per lb., while for the same quality of meat the butchers are charg- ing 11d. The Dublin grand jury on Wedneeday ignored the bill sent up against Mr. Charles Henry James, assignee of the Court of Bankruptcy, charging him with fraudulently ap- propriating considerable sums of money standing to the credit of bankrupts' estates. Two colliers, named Buckley and Loftbouse, of Leigh, found a tattered old vest lying near a field-path on Sunday. One pocket was stitched up, and on opening it they found notes of £7OO value. The men retained the nctes, but in- formed the police of their discovery. The Roma reports the discovery of a new volcano in Sicily by an officer of police stationed at Ficuzra, in the province of Palermo. He had noticel for some evenings in euccession a fire burn, so.newhat fitfully, on a hill some miles away in the country, named Busambre. Fanny Clarke, the daughter of a labourer at High Wych, on the borders of Hertfordshire, knocked a knife off the table, and in endeavouring to catch it she overbalanced her- self, and fell, alighting on the blade of the knife, which entered her side, and causing a wound so serious that she afterwards died. Feme.—Nenaow ESCAPE —A disastrous fire occurred on Tuesday morning in a public-house at North Shields. A police inspector discovered the fire, and got the water engine, and the flames were soon subdued. Two servants and three children were in bed asleep in a room filled with smoke. They were rescued and lowered to the street by means of the bedclothing. THE CLAIMANT AND HIS WIPE.—The South Stoneham Board of Guardians on Tuesday had a long discussion on the chargeability of the Claimant's wife and her two illegi- timate children. A letter was read from the Claimant repu- diating his liability, and stating that proceedings were about to be commenced against the woman in the Divorce Court. The Beard resolved to summon the Claimant before the magistrates. MRS. WELDON AGAIN.—At Marlborough-street Police Court, on Thursday afternoon, Mrs. Weldon was committed for trial on a charge of publishing a defamatery libel con- cerning M. Jules Riviere. The alleged libel was contained in a letter to M. Riviere's solicitors, in which she accused him of stealing a document belonging to her at the Old Bailey trial. The defendant was admitted to bail on her own recognisances. THE NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY WORKS AT CREWE.— The railway works at Crewe were closed on Saturday, and will continue to be closed on Saturdays and portions of Mondays until further notice. The wage sheet far Crewe will, by these means, he reduced about £l,OOO per week. The railway company have extended the same notice to the carriage works at Wolverton, where some 2,000 men are em- ployed, and also the shops at Carlisle. SECESSIONS TO THE CHURCH OF ROME.—The Weekly Register announces that within the last few days three clergymen have left the Anglican for the Roman commu- nion. These are the Rev. W. Southerden, curate of St. John's, Torquay, and formerly a worker with Mr. Lowder at London Decks; the Rev. Owen C. H. King, curate of Llantarnan, Monmouthshire; and the Rev. C. A. Burleigh Hart, formerly curate of Carrington, Lincoln- shire. PROPOSED GOVERNMENT PROSECUTION OP A LAND LEAGUER.—The Government have decided to prosecute Mr., Jasper Pyne, a recently selected Nationalist cendidate for I county Waterford, for a speech delivered some weeks ago at a League meeting near Clonmel. In the course of his speech, in presence of the Government reporter, Mr. Perna advocated the extermination of landlords and land grabbers, as being supporters of British rule and the oppressors of the Irish people. Sta R. CROSS ON THE ARTIZANS' DWELLING? ACT. Sir R. Cross, on Tuesday, at Liverpool, opened a large block of buildings constructed at an expense of £20,000 by the Liverpool Corporation under the Artizens' Dwellings' Act. Sir Richard, alluding to the Artizens' Dwellings' AM, said by its operation 30,000 persons were housed in Loadon, and his object in passing the Bill through Parliament ten years ago was to enable municipalities to do what private indi- viduals could not accomplish at one sweep—make property wholesome and habitable. SERIOUS AFFRAY WITH A ZITLII.—A. Leicester butcher, named Hubbard, is lying in the Leicester Infirmary suffer- ing from injuries sustained in an affray with a Zulu. The Zulu was performing in a ebow at the fair, and was going through a mimic fight, when Hubbard, being suspicious that the man was painted, wetted his finger and touched the Zulu on the back. The Zulu immediately leaped with a shout at Hubbard, and plunged his assegai into his face, inflicting a serious wound. which, it is feared, will entail , the loss of an eye The Zulu was secured, and Hubbard I taken to the Infirmary THE GORDON PATENT HURRICANE LAMP.—The Iron- monger says :—" We consider the ' Gordon ' Lamp well wean attention at the hand, of the trade. It is a new patent, and the manufacturers are Messrs. Thomas Rowatt and Sons, of Edinburgh, and Radeworth-street, City-road, Lon- don, E.C. In the first place, it is far more convenient for lighting and trimming than the ordinary pattern ; as, in- stead of having, for trimming the wick, to raise the top, remove the wire guard, and pen take the globe away, the only thing necessary is to release a catch, and the guard, globe, and gallery can then be turned over together on the 'binge. Taking the article in its entirety, it is simple in construction, gives a good light, is well made and durable, gives no trouble in lighting and trimming, and is withal sold at a moderate price." MURDER CASES IN LONDON.—At the Central Criminal Court, London, on Wedneaday, Mary Catherine Bicknell, 28, was indicted for the murder of her two children at 59, Edithna-street, Stockwell. It was not denied that the pri- soner, who had been previously in an asylum, was insane at the time the deed Was committed, and, evidence to this effect having been given, the jury at once found accordingly. The Judge ordered the prisoner to be detained during her Majesty's pleasure.—At the same court, Martha Howard, 27, was indicted for the murder of her child Gertrude. Mr. Poland, who prosecuted, stated that the prisoner bad been examined by a doctor, and there was no doubt that she was not in a fit state to plead to the indictment. Evidence was given as to the prisoner being in an unfit state of mind to plead, and the jury found to that effect. The prisoner was ordered to be detained during her Majesty's pleasure.—At the same court, Mary Ann Woods, 37, was found guilty of the attempted murder of her child, aged seven years, at Norwood, and was sentenced to seven years' penal servi- tude. THE ARMSTRONG ADDUCTION CASE.—At the opening of the October sessions of the Central Criminal Conrt, on Monday, the Recorder, in charging the grand jury, said that one case would come before them, against five defen- dants, which had attracted a good deal of public attention. 'The defendants would be charged, not under the new Act but by the old law, with taking a child named Eliza Arm- strong by force-and fraud from the custody of her parents without their consent All the defendants, except one, were also charged with conspiring together to take away the child in question, and they would also be charged with in- decently assaulting her. The child appeared to have been taken possession of in an extraordinary manner, and to have been taken away to several places ins most mysterious way. There appeared to be no doubt that the child was obtained possession of irir a false story, and this, if proved, would amount to fraud. With regard to one of the defendents who had published certain statements in the Pall Mall Garette, his aoswer to the charge was that nothing fraudu- lent or improper was intended to be done, but that, as the statements he had published had been disputed, his object was to show that such things could be done. It was his duty to tell them that this was in law no answer to such a charge. What the law said was that a child should not be taken away from the custody of its parents without their consent, and although such a defence would no doubt operate with regard to the question of punishment, the as- sertion that what was done was done from a good motive was no answer to the charge, and he directed them to return true bills against all the defendants upon all the counts of the indictment. On Tuesday, the grand jury in the Eliza Armstrong case found a true bill against all the defendants. MR H. R. THE NEWTON DIVISIoN. silt R. A. CROSS AT NEWTON. Sir Richard Assheton Cross, the Conservative candidate for the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire, com- menced his political campaign on Saturday, by addressing the electors in the Town Hall, Newton. There was a crowded attendance, and the proceed- ings were of an enthusiastic character, though there were several Liberals present who occasionally expressed their dissent from the opinions of the speakers. When Sir Richard Cross made his appearance on the plat- form he was received with prolonged cheers. The chair was occupied by Mr. Marcus Brown-Werothead, of Newton, chairman of the Conservative Association for the Newton Division, and he was supported by Lord Gerard (Ashton- in-alakertleld), Sir Thomas Edwards Moss (Otterspool), Sir Gilbert Greenall, Conservative candidate for Warrington, Captain Withington (Culcheth Hall), Messrs. John Pearson, J.P. (Gollsorne Park), W. Pilkington (Roby Nall), J. E. Pardey (Newton), T. P. Royden (Liverpool) Jec. There were also present—the Rev. Canon Hopwood (Winwick), Captain Beton (Lowton), Dr. Hannah (Ashton), Mews. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., W. Richardson (solicitor, Bolton), B. B. Glover, J. 0. Swift, C. H. F. Borron, W. Valiant (Ashton), J. W. Thorpe, G. Clarke, T. Jackson (Havdock), dec. I he Chairman explained that the appearance of a candidate who was claiming to be their representative in Parliament was to them a matter of great importance, and alluded to the importance of thoroughly understanding his views on the questions of the day. He believed that the experience, and the knowledge, and the admitted administrative ability, eoupled with the inviolable integrity of a gentleman like Sir Richard Cross—(cteeert9—were such as must commend themselves to their good opinions. (Hear, hear.) His principles seemed to be those of maintaining the institutions of the country intact—(hear, hear)—institutions that were the boast and envy of other great nations—(applause)— and he thought that the constituency which had previously shown a robust confidence in him would not now think that he was one likely to lead them astray—to betray either their own, individual best interests or in any measure jeopar- dise the interests of this great country. (Cheers.) It be- hoved them as electors to be very careful whom they sent to Parliament, and he thought they would say that the in- stitutions to which he had alluded should be preserved in their inteerity, and that they would send gentlemen to re- present them who would support in office the present Go- vernment, which now commanded the respect of foreign na- tions (Cheers.) They would agree with him that the Government now in power were not anxious to destroy these' institutions, though at the same time they were most will- ing to ameliorate the constitutional laws by which we had been hitherto controlled, and to which every reasonable person, even from the Crown to the meanest subject of the land, had heretofore been amenable. (Cheers) Sir Richard Assheton Cross remarked that they had met on a matter of the greatest importance, and went on to say that since he first entered Parliament in the year 1857 with the exception of a few years that he lived in the midst of the Newton Division, he had done his best serve the country in Parliament. (Applause ) He asked for the free votes of a free people, as everybody might now give hi 3 vets exactly as he liked, without any apprehension of suffering or loss, and Proceeded to say they were to fight the battle as to what principles the country should be governed under during the next six years, and that was a question which vitally con- cerned every one of them, especially the workingmen. Some public speakers on the other side had said that work- ing people should not trouble themselves about foreign affairs, but give their votes according to their thoughts about domestic legislation alone. He ventured to say that persons who made a speech of that kind were grievously wrong, and were grievously misleading the people of Eng- land. He wished to point out that foreign affairs were of the most viral importance. He pointed out that one of the duties of the foreign. office was to keep at peace with other nations and to improve in every pessible way our trade and commerce abroad, and alluded to the great importance the security and safety of India was to this country, which he said we were bound by every tie of hon- our to protect. It was to our interest as well as honour to protect there, because we had in India one of the great mar- kets of the world. What we had to do was to act up to the responsibilities of the Empire which we possessed, and to remember that those responsibilities Were oars, and that we were responsible for the good government and the happi- ness and welfare of all the people of this enormoua empire of ours, who were bound to us by those ties, and th it if we were to give up protecting and welcoming all those persons so bound to us we should be relioquishine the first princi- ples of duty which ought to govern any St ite throughout the world. But if we were thus to hold our place before the world it was absolutely essential we should be ourselves) a united people, and these islands and thie United Kineelom should be known to the world as one. There were some par- sons who, be thought, pursued a very misguided policy, and who wished to a great extent to seperate Ireland from this country. He did not think they could possibly have reflec- ted what their position would be if they could achieve their object, and how very much Ireland in the long run would suffer through being separ- ted from the rest of the United Kingdom. (Applause.) Another portion of the matter that must be considered in relation to Ireland was this, that there must be. if we are to piosper at all, abeelute security for property, for capital, and for the individual freedom of every person in the cons. try. That was what Englishmen possessed, and that was what we wished every part of our Empire to possess, and that was what the Government were determined, se far as they were able, that Ireland should have;, that it should have perfeet justice, but that there -ought to be perfect liberty for all the people. Sir Richard' proceeded to urge the irnpertance of this country neglecting no opportunity to draw closer to her in the bonds of true fellowship the great colonies across the seas who claimed kinship with us. Turn- ing to home questions, he avowed his-intention of resisting ' any attempt to interfere with the Church of England. His , belief, however, was that the people of England would neither deatroy the House of Lords nor disestablish the Church. (Cheers.) On the subject of free education he was of opinion that it was just as reasonable to demand. free food and free clothing as free education. It seemed to him also that the working man would be demoralised and would feel pauperised if the State were to take his child and edu- cate it at the expense of others. With reference to trade depression, he denied that there was any desire on the part of the Government to re-establish Protection. There were grave questions to be considered by the Commission that had just been appointed—how far depression was owing to over-production or to the high tariffs of other nations. As there were probably persons present interested in mines, Sir Richard stated that the Royal Commiesion on accidents in mires was likely soon to present its report, and then no time would be lost by him,, if still Home Secretary, in giving legislative effect to those recommendations which were calculated to tend to the protection of life or limb of these engaged in the hazardous enterprise of mining. With regard to county government,. it was the intention of the present Government, if returned to power, to bring in a bill immediately for the purpose of reforming the present system of local government. In conclusion, he had to say that he was for maintaining unimpaired the institutions of Church and State and our constitution of Queen, Lords, and Ceramohs, under which we had attained greater freedom than any other nation. He confidently placed himself in the bands of the electorate. He came to them as an old and, he hoped, a tried servant, and 80 long as they chose to send him to Parliament be would go on in the same way that he had hitherto done. (Cheers.) Mr. John Pearson moved—" That Sir Richard Asehetou Cress, G,C.P ,is a most fit and proper person to represent Newton Division in Parliament, and this meeting pledge, I itself to use every endeavour to secure his return." (Ap- plause.) rfe said he was sure Sir Itchard had not promised a single thing that he did not intend to perform, and he asked them to contrast such a speech as they had beard with effusions which had emanated from Radical plat- forms. Mr. Joseph Catterall (Earlestown) seconded the resolu- Goo. He was quite prepared to say that the working-men ' of the district would vote according to their honest convic- tions—(applause)—and he asked them to pe. Sir Richard Cross ae•amst Colonel McCorquodale. Each man should do his best to convince them that he was in the right, and he (Mr. Catterall) asked them to give their votes for the man whom they were satisfied was right. Let Sir Richard stand on his merits and he felt certain he was bound to be , returned. (Applause.) Mr. 'l' B. Royden, in a short address, said that it would be seen that the delusive promises—glittering as they did and partaking of the character of the gold sometimes tnanu- factored at Birmingham—of a particular section of the Liberal party would prove as delusive and would be as un- fulfilled as the promises made by that party when it came into office. (Cheers) On the motion of Sir Thomas Edwards-Moss, a vote of thanks was passed to the chairman, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT RALNHILL,
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT RALNHILL,

A meeting of the supporters of Colonel Gaorge MCCorquo- dale,..J.P , the Liberal candidate, was held in the Naeional Schools, Raitibill, on Monday evening, when there was a crowded attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr, G. W. Rawlins (Rainhill), who was supported by the Rev. James Johnston, Mr. C. M. Percy (Labour candidate for the Inca Division), Messrs. W. Evans, of Wavertree, former- ly of Rainhill), P. Hall (Earlestown), Cr. H. Barker, Richmond (Liverpool), H. D. Maitland, W. E.. T. Howard (Earlestown), rlm. The proceedings throughout were of a very enthusiastic character. The Chairman announced that a telegram had been re- ceived from Mr. Charles Pilkington, and a letter from Mr. W. C. Rawlins, both of whom regretted their in sail ity to be present. He congratulated the householders of the dis- t, ict upon the latest of Liberal triumphs—the extension of the suffrage to all householders in the counties and the re- distribution of seats. They were of the greatest importance to them, and were the last of a long series of reforms thaL had been brought in by the Liberals, all tending to the liberty of the subject. (Applause.) He cautioned the elec- tors against the Tory party, whom he said were claiming credit for having passed those measures. IMPORTANT FARMING CASE. A case of some interest to farmers came before his Honour Judge Houlkes at Warrington County Court on Monday. It whs one adjourned from the sitting of the Court on the previous Thursday, and occupied the attention of the judge the whole of the day. The action was brought by John Johnson, a retired farmer, against Mrs. Webster, of Sankey, to recover damages for breach of covenant in a lease of the farm from the late owner, Mr. Hughes, to Mrs. Webster's husband, now deceased, which lease expired on the Ist of May last. When the case first came before his Honoar, Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Sparrow, Barrister, Liver- pool, represented the defendant.—Mr. Longton, in opening the case, stated that the covenants in the lease which were complained of as having been broken were those to cultivate the land according to the course of husbandry adopted generally in the neigh- bourhood, and the covenants to bring manure on the land and keep the land in good " heart " and con- dition. Before witnesses were called, Mr. Sparrow contended that the benefit of the covenants under the lease did not pass with the reversion to Mr. Johnson, and also that the covenants which were said to have been broken were not such as to put him in a position to take advantage of them. After considerable argu- ment and citation of eases, his Honour said that he felt in some doubt about the matter and would not then decide the matter. Plaintiff having been examined in support of his case, the court adjourned. When the. case was re- sumed on Monday, Mr. Carver, barrister, Liver- pool, instructed by Mr. Longtcn appeared for the plaintiff.—On behalf of the plaintiff, Mr. Joseph Ciiffe, Whitley Hall; Mr. George Bawling, Warring- ton ; and Mr. James Warburton, Dallam, gave evi- dence that the covenants had been broken, they hav- ing inspected the farm in question, which, they averred, was damaged by bad cultivation. A legal contention then arose as to wheV4er Mr. Johnson was the assignee of the reversion, as it appeared that there was a second lease of the farm for seven years com- mencing from the date of expiration of the old lease. —His Honour said that he felt in doubt as to whe- ther or not the lessee was not the reversitnary of the old lease, but, after carefully citing the case of Smith v. Day, he decided that the plaintiff was the assignee of the reversion under the old lease, and that he would be in a position to claim 'damages for breach of covenants. This being decided the defendant was then examined in support of her case, and denied that the breaches of covenant had taken place. Her evi- dence was supported by that of Mr. Willies,' Halsall, auctioneer, Presoot ; Mr. Woolfall, Penketh and Mr. John Baker, farmer, Sankey. His Honour then decided that the covenants had been broken. He remarked that it was a very difficult thing for him to estimate the damage to the reversion to which Mr. Johnson was entitled, in consequence of the second lease coming in operation immediately after the determination of the first lease. After.oonsidera- tion he gave judgment for the plaintiff for £2O and costs,

div.head: SUSPECTED MURDER AT WARRING
div.p: SUSPECTED MURDER AT WARRING
TON.

At Warrington Borough Court, on Thursday, an Irish labourer named John Scanlen was brought up before Major Litton and Councilor Platt, ' and charged on suspicion with having, in company with others, murdered Michael Ward, also an Irish la- bourer, in Arpley-walk, on or about Saturday, the 10th inst.—Mr. Hunt (chief constable) said that he had received a letter from Superintendent Leigh- ton, of the .Altrincham police, in regard to a man named Michael Ward being missing. The letter stated that on the 10th inst. Michael Ward and Jno. Byrne, Irish labourers, in the employ of Mr. James Davies, of Bollington, went to Warnngton to make purchases. Byrne, the letter stated, said that Ward was badly beaten by John Scanlen and five or six others, on Friars-green, Warrington, and that Michael Ward had not been seen or heard of since. It appeared, Mr. Hunt said, that the missing man Ward was a farm labourer, single, aged about 26, was about sft. 7in. in height, had light brown hair, and wore whiskers. He was a native of Galway, and came to England in March. Scanlen was also a native of Galway, the two families living within about two miles of each other when at home in Ireland. Prisoner, his brother, and his father had been working for Mr. Yates, farmer, for the summer end. On the Saturday night in question Ward and Byrne, having made their purchases, were on Friars Green about midnight when a bother took place. Byrne would tell the Bench that he saw the prisoner strike Michael Ward on the head with his fist. Prisoner's father also attacked Ward, striking him right and left. Ward fell to the ground, and was badly used. Byrne saw him get up and run along Arpley-walk, leaving his hat behind, and that was the last that was seen or heard of him. In consequence of his friends being unable to get any news of Ward, the matter was reported to the police. Inspector Spinks on Wednesday went to the Bull's Head public-house, where he saw prisoner, and also as- certained that the father was in the house. The letter received from the Altrincham police did not say anything about the father, and consequently the Inspector only went to prisoner and asked him to walk to the Police Station. They had evidence that no sooner had John Scanlen set out to walk to the Police Station than the father left the house, fetched his clothes from his lodgings, and left the town by train, which was very suspicious. He should mention that Ward's brother, Owen, used to lodge with prisoner, who was sent to prison for a month on a charge of stealing .a half-sovereign belonging to Owen Ward, which might account for a grievance between the two. He should ask for a remand for further inquiries to be made.--John Byrne was then called and spoke as to the struggle on Friars'-green. He said that prisoner's father beat Ward while he was lying on the ground. A woman told him that she had seen Ward go down Arpley walk. Witness went after him, but came back and found Ward's hat on the ground. Examined by the Chief-constable, witness said he had known the pri- soner twelve months. The missing man was under the influence of drink when the row took place.— Inspector Spinks said after receiving instructions from the Chief-constable he went on Wednesday morning to Friars-green and made inquiries. Going afterwards to the Bull's Headin Bridge-street with Police-sergeant Rowbottom, he saw the prisoner drinking with several other men, and he apprehen- ded him. He asked prisoner when he saw his father last, to which he replied, "On Sunday." After cautioning the prisoner to be careful what he said, prisoner said, "1 knciw what you are taking me up for ; it is about Michael Ward." Subsequently Pri- soner said," It's not me, to tell the truth ; my father kicked and struck him." Witness then charged him with having killed and murderecLMichael Ward on the 10th October, and he replied, "All right witness can tell if I lifted a hand to him. John Byrne was there all the time. Ward was looking for me in Friars-gate that night to kill me. Peter Garrity is witness to that. I never saw Ward till I saw him walking down Mill-lane towards Arpley Station." Witness added that he never said a word to the prisoner about Ward going down there, and those .Were the exact words he made use or.—Pri- soner was remanded until Monday.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The East of Europe is still in a condition of painful unrest. But as yet there has been no overt act of war. At the close of last week, there were rumours pointing to the actual advance of the Servian army across the frontier, whilst the I Bulgarians were reported to be marching upon Adrianople. These reports, happily, proved untrue, andthings remain much as they were last week. The situation cannot be said to be without danger, as long as three nations are armed and daily threaten each other. But there is, nevertheless, in well informed circles a strong indisposition to believe in the imminence of war. It is reported to-day that all the Powers are now agreed on the main points respecting the Bulgarian difficulty. Prince Alexander is to remain established in his princi- pality of Bulgaria, and is to have added to his dignity the position of Governor General of Eastern Roumelia. At the same time the union of the two provinces is forbidden, each to have its separate administration. This is a hollow compromise that cannot be expected to last very long. But it may serve its purpose in averting an immediate war. The Conservatives are now fully alive to the opportunity provided for them by the apprehensions of good churchmen. They have long been in want of a cry. Now they have got one. It is the old familiar shout, "The church in danger." They are by every means in their power endeavouring to in- duce Liberal churchmen to vote against Liberal candidates at the coming elections, and so avoid the disestablishment of the church. It is a mar- vellous thing that among grown men of average in- telligence such tactics should have any effect. It is as clear as daylight, and scarcely required Mr. Chamberlain's-specific declaration on the point, that the disestablishment question will not be dealt with, in the new Parliament. Sufficient for the day is tha uneasiness-thereof, and it will be time enough for Liberals who are churchmen first to vote for Conservative candidates when a Parliament is elec- ted with a mandate to deal with the church, as the Parliament of 1868 was with respect to the Church' of Ireland. In spite of this plain fact, there is no doubt that a really considerable proportion of Liberal churchmen are turning an attentive ear to the Conservative cry, and that many votes will be lost to Liberal candidates at the coming election because of the conviction that at some indefinite time in the future Liberals will unite in disestab- lishing the church and probably transferring its funds to establish a system of free education. Affairs in Ireland do not improve. The Land Leaguers are using the weapon of boycotting with impunity, and piteous stories come from the coun- try of innocent men ruined for the sole crime,of having taken a farm from which a tenant who could not or would not pay his rent had been evic- ted. A powerful association has been formed to counteract the' influence of the League. It will have a hard fight, but if it can make any stand at all its success is assured. Last week I gave some personal particulars about Prince Waldemar, of Denmark, and Princess Marie (as she is called in the newspapers though known in her family as Amelie) daughter of the Due (If Chartres. On Tuesday the civil marriage ceremony took place in Paris, and to-day the religious ceremony followed at the Chateau. Amongst the royal . personages present was the Prince of Wales, whp must have regarded with peculiar interest this country home of the Orleans Princes. It was forty-two years ago on the 2nd of September since the Queen and Prince Albert arrived at the Castle, the guests of Louis Philippe, King of the French. A greet deal has happened since then. But it must seem to the princes of the House of France that something of their old glory is returning to them, when in their father's castle they entertain crowned heads and heirs of great kingdoms. As I mentioned last week, this alliance is a most favorable One for the Orleans family, uniting them directly with the royal families of England, Russia, Denmark, and Greece. The visit of -her son to Chateau d'Eu would recall to the queen many tender recollections of a period when she was in the full sunshine of her married life. It was upon the occasion of this visit that the Mayor and Aldermen of Southampton distinguished them- selves. The Queen and Prince Albert left Southamp- ton in the "Victoria and Albert," then a spick and span yacht just launched. It was a very wet day, and the pier was flooded by the rain. When the carriage dre* close up to the pier the mayor, taking off his crimson gown, laid it down over the mud. The Aldermen made haste to follow his example, and so tkocaromitntkivialfisvfeaked,&9ls.l2m, balm „Da happy thought and brought the mayor much fame. Poor Jumbo has been made the occasion for an action for libel. An American paper, 'called the Sunday Globe, printed a circumstantial story purport- ing to give the true narrative of the death of the mighty elephant. According to this Jumbo, was, by Mr. Barnum's direction, purposly got in the way of the train, though with what object it is difficult to understand. Mr. Barnum, in the course of a long and active life, has done many strange things to keep himself and his show before the public. It is possible that he would not object to this charge if he were able to show that the alleged murder was a very smart trick. But he sees his opportunity in theindiscretion of the Globe. An action for libel in connection with the name of Jumbo would be an I excellent advertisement, however it might end. Ac- cordingly he has brought an action for libel against the paper, claiming damages at £lO,OOO. The suit is to be heard in the October term of the American courts, and any day the telegraph may flash news of the result. A friend of mine who has been spending a little holiday in Normandy comes back with a charming story, which has the advantage of being true. He himself does not speak French, but strong in he linguistic resources of his wife he adventured the journey. One night in Rouen he went out by him- self to buy a box of matches. He conducted the transaction successfully up to a certain point. See- ing a box of matches on the counter he took it up, laid down a penny, and turned to go; whereupon the lady at the counter with growing excitement said, "Mass, non. Monsieur? (Jest eras sous—qui= centimes." The Briton, thinking the lady was making some remark about the weather, nodded pleasantly and said, "Bong swam." Then the Frenchwoman in despair produced from the till a sou, which she placed on the counter and pointed to. In a moment the Briton saw his mistake. The box of matches was only a half-penny, and here was the honest woman giving him the change. So he took up the sou, put it in his pocket, and again turned to go. Here the excitement reached the highest pitch. The lady addressed him at length, and with growing animation. But it was chiefly by signs and gesticu- lations that he gathered that in France the little box of wax matches which we buy in London at two and sometimes three for a penny cost three half- pence, one-third of which is an imperial tax. It is only a fortnight ago that the jail of the Old Bailey was delivered, and the criminal assize opens again with an unusually heavy calendar. There are 134 prisoners awaiting their trial, and the charges are very serious. There seems to have been an unparalleled recrudescence of crime. The calen- dar shows 15 cases of forgery, 13 of burglary, 4 of bigamy, 4 of libel, besides many under the new Act. Indeed, considering the numerous paragraphs about unlawful assaults on girls with which the papers have recently been abundantly supplied, the capital shows to greater advantage than the pro- vinces. There are only five of these charges in the present calendar.

' RESUMPTION o WORX BY TER Winslow COLLIERS.— After a struggle which has been prolonged for nearly three months, the miners at the Whiston Collieries.declared their Intention of resuming work on Monday. The dispute ;nose with respect to the use of riddles with meshes of a certain size, and the men declared that it was impossible for them to earn anything like a fair wage if they adopted them Toe proposals which have been accepted have come from the colliery managers, and are to the effect that in every Part of the pits the riddles will he withdrawn, sivs and ex- c.pt those parts in which the water is following the coal. The met, ale to be paid at the old rate of remuneration— is 61 per ton, and the check-weighman at Carr' e Colliery is to be permanently suspended, as it appears that be has made himself obnoxious to the men. Ceattfs COLLIERY DtwerTE.—Matt-rs in this unfortunate disagreement are not yet settled; though on Thursday week there see med a f prospeot, as the .propriet,,rs acceded to the men" terms so far as ti withdraw the hand-riddle. hut the checkweighroan, John Fegan, was not to return.. A meeting was held, and ft,gan submitted to a ballot being taken aa to whether the men were to stand by bim. The reenit wee that a majority of four votes decided against Fogsn. who ls to be appointed sub-agent to. the Mine& Federation in this district. On the men presenting them- elyes at the colliery on the Frifix, seven day wage men who had gone out the previous week and joined the men on strike, were refused work. Other men found that they were not to get their old places. and considering that they were not being well treated they met again on Saturday and by the advice ot Mr. Samuel Woods they determined not to resume work until the full terms of the agreement are car- ried out.

Do not suppose that I look upon the future of farmin4 in England gloomily. 1 have a strong faith that in the Com- mons House of Parliament men will be found from time to time who, by their courage and patriotism, backed be- an intelligent electorate, will devise such laws as will bring about a happier and more contented kingdom.
