work, by whomsoever carried on' , had endeared —him to all classes. Daring the 15 years of his episcopacy he was the leading spirit in every movement in Manchester of a philanthropic and social cheracter. He gave generous personal and financial help freely, both within and without the Church of ngland ; and he was regarded as a friend by every religious denomination, so much so that be was more than once spoken of as "the Bishop of all denominations." His activity in Church work was marvellous. The Bishop , leaves a widow, the daughter of Mr. John Shute Duncan, of Bath, to whom he was married only five years ago. At all public buildings flags were flying on Thursday at half- ' mast. It is expected that the funeral will take place on Tuesday next in Berkshire, where the Bishop's mother, to whom he was devotedly attached, is interred. " Men of the Time" says that the Right Rev. James Fraser, D.D., Bishop of Manchester, son of Mr. James Fraser, late of Heavitree, Exeter, was born at Presthury, near Cheltenham, in 1818. He was educated at Bridgenorth School at Shrewsbury. under Dr. Butler, and at Lincoln College, Oxford. He obtained the Ireland scholarship in that University in 1839, and took his B.A. degree the same year, gaining a first•cl ass in classics. 1n.1140 he was elected a Fellow of Oriel College. He acted as tutor there for five" years, and then, in 1847, accepted the college living Of Cholderton, in Wiltshire which he exchanged for Upton Nerver, near Reading, in 1860. During his connection with the diocese of Salisbury, be became chars- lain to the late Bishop Hamilton, Chancellor of Salisbury Cathedral, one of its prebendaries, and chaplain to the Salisbury Diocesan Training School. Mr. Fraser was select preacher in the University of Oxford in 1854-56, and again in 1862-64. He took an active part in connection with education under tbe Duke of Newcastle's Commission in 1858.60, to which he presented a valuable "Report on! Elementary Education in England." He was also assistant commissioner in the Schools Inquiry Commission of 1865, to which he reported on the educational systems of the United Otates and Canada. This latter report, which fills a, bulky volume, was reprinted at Sydney, in 1868, by order of the Legislative Assembly of New South Wales. I Mr. Fraser was nominated a member of the corn- ' mission appointed in 1867 to inquire into the employ-, rnent of women and shildren in agriculture. In January, 1170, be was selected by the Prime Minjster, Mr. Gladstone, to succeed the late Dr. Prince Lee in thk bishop- ric of Manchester. He was accordingly consecrated Match 15th,, 1870, having, on the third of the previonsi month, been created D.D. at' Oiford by diploma. His lordship is the author of "Six Sermons preached before the University of Oxford," 1855; "The Revised Code of the Committee of Council on Education, its principles, tendencies, and de- tails, considered in a letter to the Lord Bishop of Salisbury; with an appendix. reviewing Sir J. K. Sbuttleworth's letter to Earl Granville," 1861 ; a charge delivered at his Primary Visitation in the Cathedral, Manchester, December 3rd.and 4th, 1872; "Cathedrals and Utilitarianism," a sermon preached at the re-opening of Chester Cathedral in 1872; a speech delivered at the great demonstration held in the Free Trade Hall at Manchester, April 14th, 1873; and of numer- ous single sermons preached on special occasions.
FREE EDUCATION.

Sir,—This question seems likely to be one of absorbing Interest in the near future. That it will be one outside mere party squabble,is a certainty. Already we see signs of nelty in thought upon this,question between those who, in general polities, beloog to Navaho camps; hence the only question of disagreement may be—how shall it be done? One of the first elements of discord will be sectar- ianism. Voluntaryism:, so deservedly pseforward by the friends of Disestablishment, will not be acceptable to the support era of Free Education, yet it•will be insisted upon by those who are anxious to spread their own peculiar shib- boleths. Hitherto the arguments urged against Free Edu- cation have been twofold, viz., monetary. or bow is it to be done? and Voluntaryism or Sectarianism, as against a pos- sible Secularism. With these I have at present nothing to do. The answer given by Mr. Chamberlain to Dr. Plum- tree is at present sufficient :--" Voluntary as well as Board schools should be at once made free, and that to meet the cost an additional grant should be made from the Consolidated Fend." Were I an acceptable adviser to the Church of England party, I should it .once say—close with this offer. Already the Radial party are saying—" The revenues of the church —i10,000,000 per annum—and the vast mis-ap- plied Trust Funds, more particularly those of the city of London, will amply suffice to abolish both School Fees and the Education Rate." Dean Plumtree in his letter to Mr. Chamberlain shows that he can see further into the future than most of his brethren, and that with his school free and his fees safe, he may possibly have a better chance of competing with the School Board. The same may be said for Roman Catholics, who may he safely trusted to accept the scheme when it is once fully understood. As the law stands at present, Roman Catholics, to gain their fees have to appeal to the Board of Guardians. This necessitates exposure, which is objectionable, while the poor attending Board schools have theirs paid out of the rates. It has often been claimed by the Radicals that they are the true Conservatives. Dean Plumtree's letter confirms this. He says "that when schools were started on the paying system they were denounced by bishops and put down by kings;" and students of history need not to be told that, "in the abbey and cathedral schools of he middle ease , ãy AlaeenlA.l4neriatitee.,„vrayvelee 'etl'Oetletverdie Mee rule, and payment the rare exception." We thus see that this portion of the Radical Programme has the constitu- tional and Conservative arguments all in its favour. I was pleased to see in your report of the proceedings of the Warrington Board of Guardians that Dr. Mackie took up the question in a practical form. Let the return the doctor asked for be made as soon as possible' and it will then be seen bow necessary it is to at once link together Compul- sory Education and Free Education. We may see how political parties will disagree upon this question' when we have the Tory, Dr. Mackie, and the Radi- cal, Mr. Chamberlain, ranging themselves upon one side, and Mr. J. Lowther, the Tory, and Mr. Derbyshire, the Liberal, ranging themselves on the other. With the two latter and their followers it may be well to have a word. Mr. Lowther says Compulsory Educa- tion Should cease at twelve. After that age we are to suppose boys and girls are fit for the mill the mine or the pit. Would Mr. Lowther like to see his own children doomed, at that early age, to turn out at early morn, to face winter's bitter storms, or, as was the case in Laocashire ere the days of refo-m set in, to run the risk of having their young limbs turned and twisted oat of all human shape by commencing work before a reasonable age? I fancy not. Maybe he has found that the agricultural labourer is becoming one too many for him, and that the education he is receiving, and is likely to receive, is clearing away the " Hodge "of other days, while in his place a man "noble in reason" appears It is strange Mr. Editor, that the opinion expressed by Mr. Lowther sloniti find its echo in Mr. Derbyshire, both having a full and familiar acquaint- ance with farm life. Sava the latter gentleman,—" tie did not know what the working classes would want next. They had got abort hours, and the school fees of their children were given them. They as much as said, 'Be idle and come here for school fees and we will give them to von.'"

I take this, Sir, as a direct insult levelled at the working classes, than whom there is not in England, nay, in the whole civilised world, a harder-working, or more self-re- liant class. But leaving this twaddle, bet yet casting our eyes over agricultural England, can anyone say education le not wanted, or that it ban been given? Education shines in A men's face and at once gives him the stamp of intelligence. Let anyone glance through the pages of pages of carricaturing Punch and say how "Hodge" is there depicted. Spindle-shanked and twisted out of all form, he resembles more a denizen of the African wilds. Is it these that opponents of Free Education want to per- petuate as the upholders of British agriculture? Look at the same journal and you have the Irish peasant, with his besotted, grinning features, from which not a spark of in- telligence gleams. Although these are caricature like- nesses, they yet speak truthfully of a neglect that is now coming home to those who have said something which is not true, when they have told us that in every village the Church of England :has placed an educated gentleman whose duty and pleasure itihas been to look after the educa- tion of the poor. How can this be when to-day the strongest argument urged by the Conservatives against the county franchise is the frightfully ignorant condition of the agricultural labourer? The Dean of Wells tells us;" The cathedrals were to be centres of educational activity and centres of evangelising mission work, and their record til, lately had been a blank. Lazarus had lain for centuries at the gates of the cathedral Dives, and was as full of sores as ever." Truer words were never spoken ; evidence is forthcoming from all sides that in cathedral cities corruption exists to such a large extant that it is impossible to form political combinations. If such is the fruit of education received under the very walls of sanctity, what must it have been in rural England where the Squire and the Parson aided by my Lady Bountiful could work out their awn sweet will? Allow me, Sir, to tell Mr. Darhyshire and all who think with him that education is required now more than ever it was. If, as agriculturalists' or as manufacturers, we are to compete successfully, and hold our own, with the world's workers a full and comprehensive education must be im- parted to the people; in agriculture, chemistry; in rfle• chanica, practical science; in both a knowledge of laws that govern supply and demand.

GERARD'S BRIDGE Mrssrox Cltuacw.—The monthly meeting of the Paving, Highway, and Sewering Committee of St. Helens Corporation was held at the Town Hall, oa Wednesday afternoon, when there were present Aldermen Johnson (chairman), Gook (mayor), Councillors Foster, Be!Ether, Wilcock, Brown, and Ellisor, Messrs. Brawls (town clerk), Bram (surveyor), and Craik (deputy town clerk). Rev. R. J. Ward attended the committee in reference to a claim which had been made upon the trustees of Gera,d's _Bridge Mission Church,for the paving of a passage in VlC- torts-street and Lerd-street, close to the mission hall. They claimed exemption on the ground that it was a r.iunday school.,—The Chairman thought that would not do—other- wise all Sunday schools might claim the same thing —The Clerk said the exemption only applied to places of worship and not schools.—The Rev. R. J. Ward did not think it was registered as a place of worship.—The Mayor thought unless it could be proved that it was registered he was afraid the charge would have to be made.—The matter was allowed to etand over to the next meeting.

- - MISSIONARY MEETING AT LYMNI.—OR Wednesday evens ing a missionary meeting was held in the Wesleyan Chapel, Lymm, in connection with the Wesleyan Missionaiy. Society. The chair was occupied by Mr. Thomas Ashton, and addresses were given by the Revs. J. MeTrirk and J Yonge (Warrington), and Mr. Brown (Lymm). Collec- tions were made Ola behalf of the Wesleyan Foreign Miseions. HARVEST SERVIRER.—On Sunday harvest thanksgiving services were held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, when the sermons were preached by the Rev. W. J. Kirk- land. A flower service was held on Wednesday evening, when addresses were delivered by Mr. H. Morris, and the R-ve. A. Kirkland and W. J. Kirkland. Mr. R. Dutton pre- sided. Recitations were given and a selection of music was renderrd 1)y the choir. Collection were made in aid of the circuit funds. _

A PRISONER'S ESCAPP.-00 Wednesday evening a person who was in custody at Knutsford Gaol succeeded in making good his escaoe. The police in various districts were warned to keep a strict look our, and it has been ascertained by the Lymm police that the min has been seen in the neighbour- hood of The'wall. He was then dressed in'his prison garb. It is stited that some labourers who were breaking stones on the ways de were interrogated by him as to the road he should take to go to Warrington. They say that they thought that his clothes, which were marked with the broad arrow, were somewhat peculiar, but they were under the impression that he must be an inmate of some workhous.. A rather amusing feature of the case is that he is said to have asked his way of a county magistrate whom he met on the road. Up to yesterday he bad uot been appre- hended.

div.head: MR. LEAD AM AT LYMM.-ENTIIUSIASTIC MEETING. . .
div.p: MR. LEAD AM AT LYMM.-ENTIIUSIASTIC MEETING. . .

On Tuesday evening a meeting in support of the candi- dature of Mr. Leadam was held in the Assembly Room, Plough Hotel, Lynam. The roOm was crowded in every part, many people being unable to gain admissien, and the audience was most enthusiastic. On Mr. Leadam enterhig the room be was greeted with vociferous cheering. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. Long, and there were also on the platform beside the candidate, Mr. L. V. Harcourt (son of the Hight Hon. Sir Wm. Harcouit), Mr. W. S. Shirley (Liberal candidate for the Doncaster division of Yorkshire), Mt. J. A. Swanwick, chairman of the Lymm Polling Dis- trict •, and many others. A letter wan read by Mr. Swanwick from Mr. G. Dew- burst, Beechwood, in which he expressed regret at his in- ability to attend, but assuring them that Mr. L.Nadatn's candidature had his hearty approval and should have his practical support. ( applause.) The Chairman said the Conservatives with the most un- blushing effrontery' which one could afford to laueh at were it not for a feeling of shame at such palitical humor- ality—(applause)—in the face of all that they knew of the past history of the Conservatives, and of their opposition to this particular measure, by speech and by action, yet directly the movement became too strong for them they turned round and said, "Oh, yes, we gave you the fran- chise" (Laughter) Such a claim was too absurd to get angry about. However, they had got the franchise, and did not mean, he hoped, to give support to the party which could performs such a piece of p-ditscal jugglery, and which tried to take the credit after the battle had been won. (Ap- plause.) Mr. L. Vernon Harcourt, who was received with cheers, moved, "That this meeting desires to express its hearty thanks to Mr. Gladstone and the late Government for the extension of the franchise, obtained only by their exertions; and that it anticipates with conficl,nce their re- turn to power at the coming general election." He de- scribed Mr. Gladstone's manifesto as having strengthened and invigorated the Liberal party and the country. It con- tained n.thing revolutionary or alarming, but was full of sympathy for the people. The present Tory Cabinet of care-takers was strutting about the country like a jackdaw in borrowed plumes, seeking admiration for its borrowed statesmanship. The endeavour of the Liberal party was to wipe away all unjust privileges, and to raise men up by ex- tending their freedom. They looked forward with hopeful- ness to the day when they would establish once and forever the doctrine of the .quality of mankind. (Loud ap- plause.) Mr. Leadam. who was received with an outburst of cheer- ing and waving of hats, said certain personal attacks had been made upon him in that neighbourhood. Personal attacks were familar Tory weapons. (Applause.) The re- port now going about was that he entered a public-house in Lymm, and depositing gold upon the counter with a re- quest for a glass of bee,-, signified that he did not require change. (Laughter.) I bare was no smoke without fire, andthe fire in tbis Ca.9o was that he did enter a publ c-hou.e to have a few words of conversation with the landlord, hut the rest of the story was an odious and foolish charge which was utterly baseless—(applause)—odious because it brought against him an accusation which was criminal, and foolish because if be as a Parliamentary candidate would be guilty of conduct like that, he should be fitter for the sanatorium at Cheadle, presided over by Dr. Mold, than for Koutsford Gaol, as prescribed by the Corrupt Practices Act, (Aga-

div.head: Xattero to Hu Mar.
div.p: Xattero to Hu Mar.
MR. ASHMEAD BARTLETrS TWADDLE.

Sir,--Just a word or two on one point of the '4 brilliant " speech at the Warrington Tory meeting. Supposing Mr. Chamberlain had pneented the poor, unemployed men, who waited upon him the other day, with a cheque for £lOO, what would have been the result? Why, every Tory news- paper throughout the country, including even the halfpenny rushlight, would have howled and shrieked about " bribery and "corruption." Surely Tory working-men are not politically hungry, or they would never be satisfied with such stone broth as that served out to them by the member for Eye. Can they not see through it ? If not, then in- deed, their " wision's limited."—Yours, (to., FELIX HOLT.

plausa and laughter.) He would give this warning to the persons whe invented these charges, they brought them- selves within the scope of the law of criminal conspiracy. (Applause.) He would add this, unless he mistook the the temper of Englishmen, the result of such charges would I recoil on the head of the party which based its strength upon I charges of that nature. The party which was destitute of a programme and unencumbered by a principle, was forced to resort for its weapons to this ignoble armoury. (Cheers.) The Conservative party talked a lot about the depression of trade, but they had been in office six months, yet trade did not revive, and we seemed to be sinking into a worse con- dition. They had appointed a Royal Commission of enquiry, it was true, upon which they had brought together all sorts of quacks, with nostrums of their own manufacture which they were anxious- to retail to the public. (Laughter ) After they had filled the commission with such men as these, they went to the accredited authorities on commercial sub- j.cts, but they naturally refused to be made members of a packed jury. They then drew together two or three noble lords to give an air of respectability to the Commission, and then, very much as 'one would throw a bone to a dog, they Invited one solitary representative of labour to a seat. (Cheers.) He was happy to know that his friend Mr. Broadhurst very wisely declined to serve on any such terms. (Cheers.) The depression of trade would be much more effectually remedied by the establishment of technical schools, by the opening out of fresh channels for British Industries in foreign countries, and by extending our rail. way system. Those were the plain but effectual remedies , for our depression in trade. (Hear, heir.) He had not yet seen the Tory candidate's address, but his suggestion was that it should be printed on two sides. On the artizan's side should be a representation of the quartern loaf marked 4d—(lacghter)—and on the other, for the farmers, a quartern loaf Id. (Cheers and laughter.) The resolution was carried, with only two dissentients, amid acclamation.

Mr. G. L. WeHord moved : "That this meeting of the electors of the Lymm Polling District hereby expresses its most hearty approval of the candidature of Mr. I. S. Leadam, and pledges itself to use every legitimate endeavour to secure his triumphant return to Parliament." (Applause.) Mr. Swanwick seconded the resolution.

Mr. Shirley supported the resolution, and said he was anxious Mr. Leadam should be a member of the next House of Co.nmons, because he did not believe there was any min better fitted to represent a constituency such as this. He would not be one of those idle politicians who went to the House of Conawans simply because it was the best club in London—(hear, hear)—but he would go there to do the work of those who sent him, and in the interest and welfare of the whole country. He had thoroughly studied the land question, the most important question of the day, and his whole career marked him out as a man who would confer lustre upon any constituency which sent him to Parliament. He had no doubt he would be returned for this division. (Cheers, and a Voice: He will that,' and laughter.) The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried, amid cheers.
A vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the pro- ceedings.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The remains of the late Lord Strathaaint were interred in the churchyard at Christchurch, Hants, on Friday, in • the presence of several thousand persons. Mr. Childers has written a letter to a Yorkshire clergy- man, in which he states that he is distinctly opposed to the disestablishment of the Church of England. A telegram from Ely last evening states that the death of the Bishop 2f Ely is hourly expected. Tbe last bulletin I issued by hi9medical attendant states that his Lordabio is gradually sinking. MR. GLADSTONE ?IND HIS CONSTITEI9NTS.—On Friday morning. Mr. R W. Campbell, W.S , Edinburgh, Mr. Glad. stone's election agent, received a letter from Mr. Gladstone, dat-d Hawarden, Thursday, stating that Mr. Campbell might now fix a time for his coming to Midlothian—not sooner than Monday the 9th November—and make arrange- ments for three meetings, one in Edinburgh, one at Dalkeith, and one at West Calder.

THE BRIGHTON &GANT CASE.—At the Old Bailey,. on Friday, the Brighton bigamy trial was resumed, when Mr. Man proceeded with his address to the jury for the de- fence. He observed that very great mistakes in identity had taken place, and therefore he did not impute perjury to the witnesses for the prosecution. He dwelt at length on the weight of evidence in favour of the prisoner, and then Mr. Horace Avory replied for the Crown. LORD R. CHURCHILL AND THE BIRMINGHAM' CREST* PLOYED.—A deputation of the Birmingham unemployed have been trying to arrange an interview with Lord Ran- ' dolph Churchill. who arrived in Birmingham on Friday to commence his campaign against Mr. Bright. The deputa- tion has, however, been informed by the Conservative As- sociation that his lordship desires the strictest privacy dur- ing his visit, an that there is to be no public demonstra- tion on his arrival. THE ARMSTRONG ABDUCTION.—The trial of Messrs. Stead and Jacques, of the Pall Mall Gazette, of Bramwell Booth, Rebecca Jarrett, and Madame Combe, of the Salva- tion Army, and Madame Maurey on charges connected with the alleeed abduction of Elie,' Armstrong commenced at the Old Bailey, on Friday, before Mr. Justice Lopes. The Attorney-'3reneral led for the prosecution. The charge of abduction was Erst taken, and as this did not affect Madame Maurev she was ordered to stand back, she being only included in the court for indecent assault, for which also Stead, Jacques, and Jarrett are indicted. Although hundreds of persons appealed for admitiance, the court, by strict enforcement of the ticket system, was not over-crow- ded. The Attorney-General, in opening his case, said that by the clause under which defendants were indict-d they would be enabled to give their own explanation in the wit- ness box, while the Judge intimated early in the case that he should rule that no motive however pure justified in- fringement of the law, and that the use of fraud invalida- ted any consent to remove a child from the parents' care. The Case will last over a week, but R.l defendants are charged with miedemenour the jury are allowed to go home nightly.

div.head: EXPLOSION AT NEWTON.
div.p: THE EXPLOSION AT NEWTON.

Additig to the report which appears on another pege, we have to state that-the work of removing the debris of the wrecked " revolver room" was continued with as much prc- greets as was possible, with a due regard to the safety of those engaged in the task. The men were directed tr) the spot where It was feared, that the man Fleming had been crashed to death, and their labours resulted in the discovery of the body shortly after twelve o'clock. Be was found lying in a portion of the demolished "poacher room," in which he had been employed. It is stated that be was last seen alive by a girl named Hannah Rigby, who was laaving her employment for the day, in the same room. She got to the top of tbe steps leading from the poacher room to the beating room, when hc bid her " good night." He then turned his back earl as the girl was walking away the explosion occurred, and the poor man was crushed.to death by the falling roof and walls. Fieming'n body. was removed from the debris, and along with Byrne's, will lie in the works until after the coroner's isqueet

The Central News underatinds that Mururo Paeht‘ the Furkish Ambutsador, on Friday presented at the Foreign Office the circular note of the Porte inviting the Powers to accredit th.ir Anthavador in Constantinople to attend a' Conference to be held in that city for the discussion of mat- ters connected with the Eastern Rouroelian difficulty. MASSACRE OF CHRISTIANS IN ANNA:M. -35,000 KILLED.

Later details of the massacre of Christians ih Annam, the first intelligence of which was published doling the heat of the electoral contest in France, and which was alleged to be a party device in favour of the Conservatives, have con- firmed the first report. It is estimated that the total num- ber of victims is no less than 35,000, only 6 000 of the Christians of the district being saved. The survivors were taken to a place of safety at Saignon. The whole of the mission property was destroyed. Two hundred and sixty churches, chapels, schools, and convents were first plun- dered and then set fire to. div.head: CHESHIRE GHOST STORY.
div.p: A CHESHIRE GHOST STORY.

Heath,Stociton li.a4lacr agitated by some ghostly phenomena. Not very long ago the public of St. Helens were startled by certain mysterious, operations at Beecham's pill manufactory that were popularly supposed to be due to supernatural agency. It will be remembered that, in spite of all precautions that could be de-' vised, large numbers of stones of a rather peculiar appearance were thrown about in all directions in the building in question, in a manner most unac- countable. Rumour spread incredible tales of the doings at this place, and large num- bers of . people collected there nightly, but the closest watching threw no light on the. mystery. The " ghost " would seem to have trans- ferred its attentions from that manufacturing Lan- cashire borough to the rural Cheshire village. Here mysterious stone-throwing, singularly similar in character, has at intervals been taking place for some days past. The particular part of the village where this has been going on is a fitting spot for the vagaries of a "perturbed spirit." It is in close proximity to the village churchyard. The scene of the operations of the unwelcome visitor is one of a row of better class houses abutting on the highroad. Instead of, in the manner of the rest of its kind, disturbing the peaceful quiet of 'timorous mortals in the darkness of night, it has not feared to brave the light of day. The first indication of its presence was the smashing of glass in the 1 greenhouse built at the back of the build- ing. Little notice was at first taken of this. it being thought that some mischievous stone- thrower was to blame, but when the firft stone was succeeded by others the temporary feeling of an- noyance gave place to one of uncomfortable anxiety. It was found that the missiles were paving stones, and that a considerable quantity of glass had been destroyed. It was then determined, if possible, to clear up the mystery. Accordingly sentinels were posted in front of, behind, and on the roof of; the house, and a strict watch kept. But notwithstand- ing the utmost vigilance, in one day—the third after the commencement of these strange doings—no. less than twelve formidable looking stones were, quietly dropped from the direction of the kitchen roof on to the greenhouse, shattering about as many large panes of glass. A day of quietude followed, but on the following( day the window smashing was re- sumed in a still more singular form. Whilst several people were watching from various points of van- tage, a sound as of breaking glass was heard in the front of the house. A rush was made to the spot, and a pane of glass was found to have been broken. The shattered glass was lying some distance away 1 from the window, and near there was.a paving stone of the same sort as those thrown at the back of the house. Appearances pointed to the theory that this stone had been thrown from the inside of the house, but the occupants say that could not be. There are sceptical' people in the neighbourhood, whose windows have been left un- molested, who persist in saying that some practical' loser has been playing a prank; but there are others- whose superstitious feelings incline them to take another view. H'owbver that may be, the glass has • been broken, and it is highly probable .that the builder who has been subjected to this indignity will have to pay the piper, and replace at his own cost the damaged property.

THE RHITH AND DEATH RATE OF WAHHINOTON. —For week ending Saturday, Oct. 17th, 1885.—The mean temperature was 442 Fahr., and therefore 3.2 degrees colder than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 33 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 17th inst., and the minimum temperature. 26 Fahrenheit, oat the •12th inst. The rainfall measured '22in. The general direction of the wind was N. During the week, which was the 42nd of the current year, 40 births and 21 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 24* per 1,000, against 16.8 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 17.5 the eor- responding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from erysipelas, 2 from. diarrhcea, • f from typhus fever, 5 fram phthisis, 1. from cancer, 2 from heart disease, 3 from brain disease, and 1 from lung disease.— Jourt H. CiimNALL, Medic-at Officer of 11ea1,411,

Mr. Isaacstein : "Make dot shentlemans who vas a clergyman twenty per cend. discoand off." Clerk: "Der sheatlemans says he viii give won-guinea for dot coat, and not a shixpence more.' Mr. Isaacatein : "Let him have dot cost, Jacob, but dond make no disooand off °' A man had a legacy left him, but it was harapered with an unfortunate condition, which he hastened to announce to a sympathising friend. The slam of £2,000 but half of it, according to the testator's wishes, was to be placed in his coffin and buried with him. But the sympathiser was equal to the occasion. CASE OF "CLAW ME. CLAW Tnaa."—A. Salvation Army Ualpuoau VMS once gea.,s ,alaaa LA. 04.4 uvn. LAS kAA • mercial.road, when his retrograde movements knocked the pipe out of a costermonger's mouth. A row would naturally have resulted, but the umbrellaed one half apologised, and then added, "But, you know, you would have had a chim- ney on your head if you had ever been intended to smoke." This gave the costermonger his opportunity. He demanded indignantly, "And do you think you was intended to walk back'ards? Why, yet feet would 'a been screwed round if yer was." He was on his knees before her, and with a voice tremu- lous with passion, he said :" Nothing shall separate us ever- more, my darling! For your sake I will beard the lion in his den! I will face death on the battle field! I will skim the seas! I will endure all hardship, all suffering, all misery !" He paused and looked eagerly at bet, with hii whole soul quivering in his eyes. "Will you do all this for the sake of my love?" said she, gazing earnestly at him. " Yes! yea! a thousand times yes!' "And if we wed," con- tinued she, flushing slightly, " will you get up first and 1 I build the fire ?" With a shriek of despair he fled. JOSH INTERVIEWS EIIMSHLF.--What iz yore favourite piece of sculpture, Mr. Billings ? The milestone nearest home.—Who do yo konsider the wisest man that haz ever lived? The one that knows the least about his nabore and the most about himself.—What do yu konsider the highest priced things in this world? Thoze things we buy, and pay I for, with repentanse.—Do yn beleave in the divinity of the Bible? I do; and bekause I kan't prove it, and no living nor ded man has ever been able to dieprove it yet.—What iz yore ideal of female buty ? That kind which you kan't exactly define, and which never undertakes todefine itself.— Will yu define a hipokrit ? One who prays to heaven fervently, and then just as fervently preys on hiz nabor.— What is the best and only real pedigree a man kan hat? The one whitch he makes for himself—one whitch he kan't inherit, nor kan't transmit.—Who is yure favourite mathe- matician? He who in summing up the good he has done, and substrakting from it the evil he has committed, kan honestly sho that he iz surnthing ahed in the arithmetik.— Will yn please to define liberty? Liberty is a komprehen- dye term, under whitch we klaim very much and possess very little.—Who are yore favourite painters? Temperance and Industry. They paint living portraits ov health, wealth, and happiness.—Are there many things in this world that money won't buy? Yes, sir, lots of them. It won't even buy the wag ov a dog's tale.—Whitch do yu konsider the most ViSoloos OV all pastitms ? LazyneFr: ; it eats up a man bi inches, and never gives bak a mouthful.—What is yure favourite piece of arkitekture ? The little red painted sklsool house, down at Pordunk, wham I lernt bow to spell, ' play tag, and worry the skool marm.—What is yure private opinyun ov a republikan form ov government? Possessing all the elements ov strength, the weakest kind ov all governments.—Who iz :lure favourite inventor? The man who invented the fust tin whissell, and established the price at a penny.—Whitch do yu koosider the most sterling quality in man? Honesty; and yet it ain't lawful tender on the streets for a loaf ov bread.—Pleaze tell me the difference between modesty and bashfulness ? One iz all silver, and the other only the plating on the spoon, which soon wears off, and shows the brass—Would yu like to live your life over again?
